bio.en: Jason Fried is co-founder and CEO of 37signals, the profitable, bootstrapped company behind Basecamp and HEY that has made money for 24 straight years with no investors, no board, and no plans to sell or go public.
bio.zh: Jason Fried 是 37signals 的联合创始人兼 CEO；37signals 是一家盈利、自筹资金的公司，旗下有 Basecamp 和 HEY，连续 24 年盈利，没有投资人、没有董事会，也无意出售或上市。

summary.en: Jason makes the case that bootstrapping gives founders far more practice at the fundamental skill of making money, and that there's far more room to build a successful, fulfilling, even more lucrative business outside the 'go big or go home' VC path that almost nobody actually wins. He argues constraints like small teams and less cash often produce better outcomes, that gut and instinct are underrated decision tools, that long-term planning is often a mistake, and that work shouldn't feel like war. The episode is a compelling alternative philosophy for building a company on your own terms.
summary.zh: Jason 提出，自筹资金让创始人更多地练习“赚钱”这一根本技能，而且相比几乎无人胜出的“不成功便成仁”的 VC 路线，在它之外有更大的空间去打造成功、充实、甚至更赚钱的事业。他主张小团队、少现金之类的约束往往带来更好的结果，直觉是被低估的决策工具，长期规划常常是错误，工作不应像战争。这期节目是关于“按自己的方式”打造公司的、令人信服的另一种哲学。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: The reason I think it's great for entrepreneurs to start bootstrapping is because they just have more practice making money, and they get better, and better, and better at the fundamental skill you need to have ultimately to run a successful business, which is to make money. Hopefully, I don't come off as encouraging everyone to be like me. I'm not saying that at all. What I'm saying is, this is a way to be. It's an alternative to what you're often hearing in our industry, which is, "Go big or go home. Raise a bunch of money and get huge, and unicorn status," and the whole thing. That's a way. Just know though that basically almost nobody makes it that way. Really, almost nobody really makes it that way, and there's a lot more room to make it, and to build a successful business, if you throw out that outlier and look at all the other places you can land as a business.
turns.zh: 我认为创业者选择自力更生发展很棒的原因在于，他们在赚钱方面积累了更多经验，并且能不断提升这项核心技能——赚钱。这项技能是成功经营企业的基础。希望我这样说不会让大家误以为我在鼓励大家效仿我。我绝不是这个意思。我想说的是，这是一种可行的道路。与我们行业常听到的"要么做大，要么回家；大规模融资、实现独角兽估值"之类的说法相比，这是一种截然不同的选择。当然，几乎没人能通过这种模式成功。说真的，绝大多数人都无法复制这种模式。但如果你抛开这种极端案例，审视商业成功的其他可能性，就会有更广阔的成功空间和更多机遇。

turns.zh: 我们不会过多谈论那些不那么重要的数据，比如收入，因为即使赚很多钱也可能导致资金链断裂。但我们会关注利润。回顾过去10年，过去24年我们每年都实现盈利。但过去10年，我们每年都能获得数千万美元的利润，这确实很棒。我们有超过10万名付费客户（这是个粗略数字），目前约有75名员工。（00:06:12）：所以，就员工数量而言，我们是一家规模相对较小的公司，但拥有庞大的客户基础和丰厚的利润，这正是我们一直坚持的经营理念。与我经常听到的那些指标不同——那些指标通常附带缩写术语，我甚至不明白其含义——我们只关注两点：赚得比花得多，保持健康的利润率，这样我们才能进行实验、尝试新事物，不必害怕可能失败的项目，并享受整个过程。这就是我们近25年来一直坚持的经营之道。而明年将是我们成立25周年的纪念年。

turns.zh: 回到刚才的话题，显然很多公司选择走风险投资路线，他们愿意长期亏损，以期未来能赚取巨额利润。所以核心理念是：尽可能快速扩张规模，然后再去盈利。你一直主张不融资，坚持自力更生。那么，当融资确实有意义时，对创始人有什么建议呢？我曾写过一篇名为《你的初创公司很可能达不到风险投资级别》的文章，试图说服人们：即使你有绝佳的创意，也不意味着它就能成为风险投资级别的企业。我感觉我们在这一点上看法一致。你对创始人有什么建议呢？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Obviously, if you're building cars, or you need a factory, or you're opening a restaurant and there's actual things you need to buy like ovens, and you need to hire people right off the bat, and you need to pay rent, you need capital. It could come from you. It could come from friends and family. It could come from an investor. It can come from a bank loan. There's lots of places to get it, but you'd need it. Software businesses though, and businesses like ours, we just make software, and a lot of people in our industry are like us in that respect. They need a couple laptops and a couple people, and it's pretty cheap. It's really pretty cheap to get going, and the margins are incredibly healthy in software, or they should be. (00:08:06): What's interesting is that Silicon Valley has found a way to make the most profitable style of business the least profitable. Software, there's no physical costs. The margin should be close to 80 or 90%. It turns out that they're barely even, most of them positive in the end, or they're just sliding by basically. I don't understand how that... Well, I do. They have too many people and they spend too much money on customer acquisition, and all that. But, it blows me away. Most businesses in the world would love to have Silicon Valley style economics, make something that doesn't cost much to make and then sell it for high prices. (00:08:50): But everyone, the corner store, the pizza shop, they wish they could do this, and they can't because they have physical products that they have to sell, and they have to buy goods, and they have to get raw materials and convert that into a pizza, and there's just costs involved with that. They can't sell it for too much because the other place down the street sells it for less. So again, I'm getting off track, but if you're going to start a business that really truly requires cash, typically capital expenditures, expensive things, hardware, whatever, of course you need that. But, I don't think you do otherwise. (00:09:20): I think it actually hurts you if you go out and think that you do, because there really is only one outcome for venture-backed companies, which is go huge. If you think about all of the space between a small business and a massive, huge unicorn-y business, there's so much room there that you could normally find your own way, and slide into a slot or a place that makes sense for you. But if you're venture-backed, you just don't even have the opportunity. You blow right past those, or they want you to blow right past those. If you don't, you wither on the vine and die essentially, and it's just too bad.

显然，如果你要制造汽车、开办工厂、经营餐厅，或者需要购买烤箱之类的设备，刚开始就得雇人，而且还要支付租金——这时候你就需要资金。资金可能来自你自己、亲友、投资者，或者银行贷款。融资渠道有很多，但资金是必不可少的。然而像软件公司这样的企业，我们只做软件开发。业内很多人和我们情况类似，他们只需要几台笔记本电脑、几个人手，就能低成本启动业务，利润空间也极为可观。

（00:08:06）：有趣的是，硅谷竟能把最赚钱的商业模式做成最不赚钱的。软件业务没有实体成本，利润率本该接近80%或90%。但现实情况是，大多数公司勉强持平，甚至出现亏损，基本是在苦苦支撑。我不明白这是怎么回事……好吧，我懂了。他们雇了太多人，还在客户获取上花费过多资金等等。但这真让我震惊。世界上大多数企业都希望能拥有硅谷式的经济模式——生产成本低廉的产品，然后高价销售。

（00:08:50）：但每个小商店、披萨店都希望能做到这一点，可他们做不到，因为他们有实体产品需要销售，必须采购原材料并将其加工成披萨，成本不可避免。他们不能高价销售，因为街边的竞争对手价格更低。所以我又跑题了，但如果你要创办一家真正需要资金的企业，通常需要大量资本支出、昂贵的硬件等，这些都是必需的。但除此之外，我认为没必要强求。如果你因此强求，反而会拖累自己。

（00:09:20）：我认为这对风投支持的公司来说反而有害，因为风投支持的公司只有一个结局——要么做大做强。要是把小企业和大型独角兽企业之间的差距考虑进来，其实有很大的发展空间，通常能找到适合自己的位置。但如果你受风投支持，就没有这样的机会。风投希望你迅速扩张，否则就会被淘汰。这太可惜了。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: We run a very different kind of business. We are focused on efficiency, we're not focused on growth. They're focused on growth. So typically, when you have a lot of people, you think you can do more things at once, and you probably can. You do more things at once, and have different offerings to different people, and different tiers, and salespeople, and all the things that build up an organization. We don't have any salespeople. We don't have 15 different versions of Basecamp. We're not after enterprise, so we don't have the enormous support costs and enormous support infrastructure required to service customers like that, and customize this and customize that to keep a whale happy who's paying you $300,000 a year. (00:11:13): We don't have any of those things. We have one price, basically. Well, we have two prices on Basecamp, one price on HEY. Actually, two prices on HEY. Two, basically. But one code base, one product we offer everybody. Let's take Basecamp for example. Nobody can pay us more than 300 bucks. I don't care how big your company is, the most you can pay us is $299, you get unlimited users. What that allows us to do is to just build one product, do a really nice job, keep it tight, and simple, and clear, and not have the complexity that comes with trying to service and satisfy so many different kinds of companies at different price levels with different price points and different expectations. That's why these companies tend to get bigger and bigger and bigger. (00:11:58): They also, frankly, build products just differently. We build products with two people at a time. So every feature we work on in Basecamp, or HEY, or whatever we're building is two people, one programmer, one designer, and they have a maximum of six weeks to deliver the feature that they're working on. Most of them are usually a couple of weeks, but they have a maximum of six weeks. So we don't get stuck in these big huge projects, with meetings with 18 people, and slow decision-making, and indecision, and complexity, and all the things that come with trying to do too many things for too many people. Now, all that said, we could still make the mistake of hiring hundreds of people because we could afford to do so. But to spend money because you have it on things you don't need is something that Silicon Valley's gotten quite good at, but we're quite bad at intentionally. I don't want to spend money on things we don't need. (00:12:49): So we think that constraints, simplicity, small teams actually are where it's at, and keep us honest, and allow us to do great work for our customer base that we know, small businesses, very tight companies like ours, and satisfy them versus trying to go after the big companies, and have to have salespeople, and have long sales cycles, and whatnot. Honestly, if you gave me 1,000 people, I wouldn't know what to do with them. We would fall apart. If you gave me 500 people, I wouldn't know what to do with them. We would fall apart. We would be a worse off company with 500 people. I'd be completely lost. So, that's the other thing. I don't even understand how they run, and the amount of layers they must need, and the amount of complexity organizationally that they must have to... The latticework they have to build up to support all that weight, is just remarkable and it's foreign to us.
turns.zh:
我们经营的是一种截然不同的业务。我们专注于效率，而非增长。他们则专注于增长。因此，当团队规模扩大时，人们往往会认为能同时处理更多事务，实际上也确实如此。团队会为不同客户提供不同服务、设置不同等级、配备销售人员等等，以此构建组织架构。但我们没有销售团队。Basecamp没有15个不同版本。我们不追求企业级市场，因此无需承担为此类客户提供支持、定制产品以讨好每年支付30万美元的巨头客户所需的巨额成本和复杂架构。（00:11:13）我们没有这些冗余。基本上，我们只有单一价格。实际上，Basecamp和HEY各有两种定价方案，但核心产品始终统一。比如Basecamp，用户最高支付额不超过300美元。无论公司规模多大，用户最多只能支付299美元即可享受无限用户权限。这种模式让我们能专注于打造单一产品，保持产品简洁明了、清晰易用，无需为满足不同价格层级、不同需求的客户而承受复杂性负担。这正是这些巨头企业越做越大、越做越复杂的根源。

（00:11:58）说实话，他们的开发方式也截然不同。我们每次只派两人负责产品开发。无论是Basecamp、HEY还是其他项目，每项功能的开发都由一人编程、一人设计，团队最多有六周时间完成任务。多数功能通常在两周内完成，但最长不超过六周。这样我们就避免陷入大型项目的泥潭——无需召开18人会议、承受漫长决策过程、纠结于复杂性等问题。说到底，即便有资金支持，我们也绝不会盲目扩张团队。硅谷擅长用钱堆积资源，但我们更倾向于精打细算。我们不想把钱花在不必要的环节上。

（00:12:49）因此，我们坚信，约束、简洁和小团队才是核心竞争力。这些原则能让我们保持专注，为熟知的客户群体——比如小型企业、紧密团结的公司——提供优质服务，而不是去追逐大型客户、养活销售团队、应对漫长销售周期等。这类复杂性对我们而言完全陌生。说真的，如果给我1000名员工，我都不知道该如何管理。他们会把公司搞垮。即便500名员工也难以驾驭。500人规模的公司只会让情况更糟。我完全无从下手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I definitely want to talk about how you operate in your way of working, 'cause it's really interesting and there's a lot companies can take away. But, I want to follow on this thread of small teams. I have a few quotes that you've shared that I love.
turns.zh: 好的。我确实想谈谈你工作方式背后的运营理念，因为这真的很有趣，很多公司都能从中借鉴。但我想先接着小团队的话题继续聊聊。我特别喜欢你分享的几句名言。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Oh, no.
turns.zh: 哦，不。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, no.
turns.zh: 哦，不。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: No, good. No, it's good. Hey, if I said it, I said it. Let's go.
turns.zh: 不，不错。没关系，说就说吧。走吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, they're awesome. They're great. Around this idea of staying small, one is, "Small is not just a stepping stone, small is a great destination itself. Also, if you think you're too small to be effective, you've never been in bed with a mosquito."
turns.zh: 不，他们很棒。他们非常出色。关于保持小团队规模的理念，有一句是：“小型化不只是垫脚石，它本身就是一个伟大的目标。还有，如果你觉得自己太渺小而无法发挥作用，那你肯定没和蚊子睡过觉。”

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Now that's not my quote. That's someone else's, to be clear.
turns.zh: 不过那不是我的名言。说清楚，那是别人说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay, you popularized it.
turns.zh: 好吧。好吧，你让它流行起来了。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: It's a great quote though.
turns.zh: 不过这确实是个很棒的名言。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Then there's one more. "You don't need to outdo the competition, it's expensive and defensive. Underdo your competition. We need more simplicity and clarity." I think a lot of these things point to, there's a few paths to success and goals for people. One is build a massively scaled, everyone's using a product like Figma and Notion, and build a venture scale, $100 billion company. Then there's this path which is, we're just going to make a bunch of profit we're going to make individually. We're going to take home a bunch of cash. We're not trying to have everyone in the world use it. I know your focus is, you call it, the Fortune 5 million versus the Fortune 500. So maybe just whatever you want to share about what success means to you, how you think about what success is for you, for the company your building.
turns.zh: 好的。还有一句。“你不需要超越竞争对手，那既费钱又防御性强。相反，要弱化竞争对手。我们需要更多简洁明了的东西。”我觉得很多这些观点都指向了成功的不同路径和目标。一种是打造大规模产品，比如Figma和Notion这样的产品，建立价值千亿美元的企业。另一种是专注于个人盈利，赚取丰厚现金流，不追求全世界都使用你的产品。我知道你的关注点是，你称之为《财富》500万强和《财富》500强企业之间的差异。所以或许你可以分享一下成功对你意味着什么，你如何看待自己和所建公司的成功标准。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: For me, it's really about, would I want to do this again? If the answer is, "Yeah, that was enjoyable. I enjoyed that. That was worthwhile. I'm glad I did that. I'd like to do that again," then it was successful. Now you could carve out some extremes there. I'm sure someone who's addicted to drugs might go, "That felt great, I should do that again." So you got to be careful with that, in a sense. Obviously, I'm not talking about that. Addiction's a whole different story. But in general, with this stuff, "That was fun. Let's do that again. That worked. Let's do that again." Or, "That didn't work. I didn't like that. That was a pain in the ass. That was too complicated. That took too long. Let's not do that again." So it really is about, do you want to do that again? That's what success is to us at a root level. (00:15:37): Now, on the business side of things, we have to be profitable. That doesn't mean that everything we do needs to be profitable. I am not driven by data, or I don't have different P&Ls for each product in a way where we're looking at them very carefully. It's in total, collectively, are we making more money than we spend? That's the only thing we ultimately look at, whether or not this product is more profitable than that product, and this is behind that, it's all the things we do. It's all the things we do. I don't even think you can actually draw lines back to everything and go, "That was worth it. That wasn't worth it." What is the value of saying thank you to somebody? Would you want to A/B test that and, if it turned out that it was worse to say thank you to somebody, would you not do that? No, you would do it because it's still the right thing to do. (00:16:28): So a lot of our things are, what feels right? What seems like the decent thing to do? What things do we enjoy making? As long as we can, at the end of the year, look back and go, "Well, collectively, more worked then didn't work," then we're okay. That's how we look at it. We don't have financial goals. We don't have OKRs or KPIs. I don't have revenue targets. I don't have growth targets, in terms of the number of customers we need to pick up this year versus last year. I don't look at any of those things. It's just, at the end, "Did we make more than we spend? We did. Then the things we did this year were worth it." That's how it goes.
turns.zh:
对我而言，关键在于：我是否愿意再次尝试？如果答案是：“嗯，那很愉快。我乐在其中。这很值得。我很庆幸自己做了这件事。我还想再来一次。” 那就意味着成功了。当然，极端情况下可能会有人说：“这感觉太棒了，我应该再来一次。” 所以对此要谨慎处理。显然，我不是在说成瘾问题——成瘾完全是另一回事。但总的来说，如果我们做某件事时会说：“这很有趣，让我们再来一次。” 或者：“这行不通。我不喜欢这样。这太麻烦了。耗时太久了。还是别再做了。” 那么关键问题就是：你愿意再次尝试吗？这就是我们对成功的根本理解。  

（00:15:37）：在商业层面，我们必须盈利。这并不意味着我们做的每件事都必须盈利。我不受数据驱动，也不会为每个产品单独制定损益表并进行细致分析。关键在于整体上，我们整体盈利是否大于支出。这才是我们最终关注的核心——无论是某个产品比其他产品更盈利，还是否值得投入资源。  

（00:16:28）：所以我们很多决策的核心在于：什么感觉是对的？什么看起来是体面的做法？什么是我们乐于创造的？只要年底回顾时能说：“嗯，整体而言，成功多于失败。” 那就说明我们做得不错。这就是我们的看法。我们没有财务目标，没有OKR或KPI。我没有收入指标，没有客户增长目标，没有去年与今年客户数量的对比目标。我从不关注这些。关键在于：我们赚得比花得多吗？是的。那今年做的事就是值得的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also have no investors. You have no board. You have no plans to go public. You have no plans to sell the business.
turns.zh: 你们也没有投资者。没有董事会。没有上市计划。没有出售公司的打算。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this book, I don't know if you've read this book called, Finite and Infinite Games.
turns.zh: 有本叫《有限与无限游戏》的书，不知道你读过没。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: No, I've not.
turns.zh: 没读过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I think you would love it. The whole premise of this book, it's like a terse, tricky, philosophical book, but it's very short. It espouses, you want to be playing infinite games to be happy in life, games that never end versus games like, I'm going to build a business and sell it. Or, I'm going to go public, that's my goal. Or, I want to achieve this promotion. You get most joy out of things that never end, like building great relationships, building a company you want to keep working at forever.
turns.zh: 好吧。我觉得你会喜欢这本书的。这本书的核心观点很简洁、很有挑战性，是本哲学著作，但篇幅很短。它主张，要想在生活中获得快乐，就要参与无限游戏——永无止境的游戏，而非像“我要创办公司然后卖掉它”之类的有限游戏。或者“我的目标是上市”，或者“我想升职”。最能带来快乐的，是永无止境的事物，比如建立深厚的关系，打造一家人人都想永远为之工作的公司。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I like that. What's interesting is, I've always thought of my career this way. When I got my first job, I was 13. I worked in a grocery store for a bit, and then I worked in a shoe store. After that, maybe when I was 15, I got a resellers license, which was this thing... This is way back in the day. I think they still exists. A company called Ingram Micro D, which had this huge thick catalog of electronics equipment. If you had a resellers license, you could buy these things at wholesale prices, then I could sell them to my friends for retail, which is almost 2x wholesale. Even though I'm not selling electronics equipment today, I'm selling software instead, I feel like I have the exact same job as I did when I was 15, that this is a long continuum of finding stuff that I like. (00:18:31): In this case today, it's building things that I like, and selling them to like-minded people who also would find them useful or those things too. So whether or not it's software, or electronics, or stereo equipment, or whatever the heck it is, or music organizing databases, it's all the same to me, and I just want to keep doing it. This is my day job. The other thing that's interesting about entrepreneurship is, sometimes there's a sense of, you can get a job or you can be an entrepreneur. Well, an entrepreneur is a job. This is my job, so I want to create the company that I want to work at, and I want to keep doing this job for as long as I can. As long as I'm useful, I'm good at it, I enjoy it, I want to keep doing that. (00:19:14): So to get in bed with an investment that would say, "In five years you have to stop doing what you're doing, you're going to get a big paycheck maybe, but you got to stop doing what you're doing because we're going to sell this business, and you're going to have to go work for this other company for two years and do their thing. Then eventually, after that's over, you'll leave and you'll go start another thing," that just has no appeal to me at all. I'd rather just keep doing the thing that I'm enjoying doing, as long as I can continue to make it work. (00:19:37): What's cool about having a company like ours, which is an independent business, we don't have to ask anyone for permission. No one can tell us no. So we can turn this into anything we want. It's this vehicle, more so than it is a software business. It happens to be, of course, what it is, but it could be something else as well. There's no limits to what it could be, and that's a fun way to go through life too, in this all-terrain vehicle which can anywhere, on-road, off-road, whatever, and you can get anywhere you need to go. That's what's really quite fun about the kind of business we have.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样做。有趣的是，我一直都是这样看待自己的职业生涯的。我13岁时得到第一份工作，先是在一家杂货店工作，后来又在一家鞋店工作。大概15岁时，我获得了经销商执照，那时候……那已经是很久以前的事了。我觉得这种执照现在应该还是存在的。当时有一家叫Ingram Micro D的公司，里面有厚厚的电子设备目录。持有经销商执照的人可以以批发价购买这些产品，然后以零售价卖给朋友，利润几乎是批发价的两倍。虽然我现在不卖电子设备了，转而销售软件，但我觉得自己现在的工作和15岁时做的一模一样——不断寻找自己喜欢的东西。（00:18:31）：现在的情况是，我在开发自己喜欢的东西，然后把它们卖给志同道合、觉得有用的人。所以无论是软件、电子设备、音响设备，还是音乐整理数据库，对我来说都一样，我只想继续做下去。这就是我的日常工作。创业的另一个有趣之处在于，有时人们会觉得，要么找份工作，或者成为创业者。嗯，创业本身就是一份工作。这就是我的工作，所以我想创建自己想工作的公司，只要我还有用、擅长这份工作、乐在其中，我就想一直做下去。（00:19:14）：所以如果投资方说"五年后你必须停止现在的工作"，也许你能拿一大笔钱，但你必须停止现在的工作，因为我们要把公司卖掉，然后你得去另一家公司工作两年。等那结束后，你再离开去创办新事业，这对我来说毫无吸引力。我宁愿继续做自己喜欢的事情，只要能维持下去就行。（00:19:37）：像我们这样的独立公司很酷，我们不需要征求任何人的许可。没人能否定我们。所以我们可以把公司打造成任何我们想的样子。它更像是一辆全地形车，而不仅仅是软件公司。当然，它现在是软件公司，但也可以是其他形式。没有什么限制。这种生活方式很有趣，就像开着一辆全地形车，可以在任何地方行驶，公路、非公路，随心所欲。这种商业模式真的很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have this term you hold, instead of a startup it's a stay up.
turns.zh: 你有这样一种坚持，而不是创办一家初创公司，而是持续经营。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yes. I'm so sick of the startups. It's cool to start a business, obviously, but I'm sick of that term dominating. Because, frankly, starting a business is actually way easier than staying in business. Now, none of it's easy, so I want to be supportive of people who are starting businesses. But they should know that that's actually not the hard part. Literally tomorrow, I can start a new business. You can come up with a name, and you can make a thing, and you can put in the app store, and you can sell it for two bucks, and you've got a business going. But, are you going to be there in two years? Are you going to be there in five years when competition rushes in? When you have employees, are you going to be there? Staying is harder than starting. So I'm here to celebrate stay ups. Plenty of other people are here to celebrate startups.
turns.zh: 是啊，我真是受够了这些创业公司了。创业当然很酷，但这个词被过度炒作让我很反感。说实话，创业比维持业务要容易得多。不过创业绝非易事，所以我支持那些初创企业。但他们得知道，真正难的不是创业，而是持续经营。明天我就能创办新公司：想个名字、开发个产品、上架应用商店、卖两美元，一门生意就成了。但两年后你还在吗？五年后竞争对手涌入时你还能坚守吗？当员工加入时，你还能掌控全局吗？坚持比创业更难。所以我来这里为那些坚持下去的人喝彩。其他人都在为创业公司欢呼雀跃。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel the same way. I always say this about newsletters, and it's also true for podcasts. Easy to start a newsletter, hard to keep it going.
turns.zh: 我感同身受。我常这么说新闻通讯，这对播客也适用。创办新闻通讯容易，维持下去难。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Totally. I've seen your newsletter fly. We have a newsletter and it's been pretty flat. I'm like, "How does he do it?" It's hard. It's really hard. It's hard to build a podcast audience. It's hard to build a newsletter audience. So yeah, starting something is really easy, but then most people end up in this plateau area, 'cause they get some initial growth, the word gets out, and they end up with 6,000 somethings, and then you're stuck there. Then it's like, "Well, do you want to keep doing this? Or, are you just high on the growth? Or, do you actually like the thing?" (00:21:42): If you want to do the thing for a long period of time, you've got to like the thing because you're going to have to endure these moments of plateaus, which is what staying up is all about. Sometimes those go down. We've had wavy years, always been profitable, but our profit's different every year. Sometimes it's more, and sometimes it's less. Sometimes our margin is more, sometimes it's less. If you compare yourself to the previous year, you can get demoralized to some degree. But I just, "What do we want to keep doing?," and then we're in it to stay in it.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。我见过你的新闻通讯火遍全网。我们也有新闻通讯，但发展平平。我就想：“他是怎么做到的？” 这太难了。做播客、做新闻通讯都难。所以创业确实容易，但多数人最终陷入停滞期——刚起步时获得些增长，口碑传播后，订阅量达到几千，但就此停滞了。这时你得问自己：是想继续做下去，还是只为追逐增长刺激？还是真心热爱这件事？（00:21:42）：若想长期坚持，就必须热爱这件事，因为你必须承受停滞期的煎熬，而这正是坚持的真谛。有时收益下滑。我们经历过起起落落，每年利润不同，有时多些，有时少些。利润率时高时低。和前一年对比，容易陷入自我怀疑。但我总会问：“我们想继续做下去吗？” 然后我们就坚持下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of enduring, you've been at this for almost 25 years now, I believe?
turns.zh: 说到坚持，你从事这行快25年了吧？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have there been periods where... I like that sigh that you just had there.
turns.zh: 有没有过迷茫期？我刚听你叹了口气。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: It's a long time.
turns.zh: 时间太长了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So maybe along that path, one, is there a point at which maybe you started going off track and you realized, "This is not what I want to be doing. Why did I do this to myself?" Then two is just, what have you learned being at this for this long?
turns.zh: 那么回顾这段历程，第一，你有没有偏离轨道过？意识到“这不是我想做的事，我为什么要这样折磨自己？”第二，坚持这么久，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I would say, over the past few years, I've had more thoughts of, "How long should I do this for?" I go back and forth. I can tell you, what's interesting is, right now, I'm probably more excited than I've been in many years. But, a year ago I was not so excited. I think that after you've been doing this for a while, you do tend to just compare, what was it like in the early days? What's it like now? All the new things that are harder weren't harder before, and now they're hard today. Do I like doing this kind of hard work, or would I rather do...? You just amass this history, and so you tend to just call back to it, and look back to it. So you opine for the early days, or you reminisce, I should say. (00:23:16): "Yeah, it was so much easier when we were 20 people." "Yeah, but we weren't doing this, and times were different, and you can't go back anyway." But, it's interesting. Next year I'll be 50. We'll be doing this 25 years. I'll have been running this company for 25 years. Part of me thinks, "Is that enough? Maybe that's enough." But right now, I'm really excited about what we're doing. We're doing some really great product work, probably the best we've done in many, many years. Launching this new thing called ONCE, which hopefully we're going to build three or so products next year under that category. I would like to write another book. We finally have another idea for another book. (00:23:53): So there's just, right now, this outpouring of energy. I'm trying to be very conscious of my energy interest. Right now, I'm getting energy from the business. There are times in the past where the business sapped energy for me. If it SAPs too much, at some point, you start to think, "Is it worth it? Do I want to keep doing this?" Right now, I'm fueled again by it. But, I don't know what it'll be like in a year from now. I really don't know. I think I'm more conscious of that than I've ever been given how long I've been doing this. (00:24:21): Also, I always have this strange fantasy, I'm always curious, "What would someone else do with this place? What if someone else could just step in tomorrow? How would they run it? No one's ever had a chance to run it but me. What would they do differently?" I'd have to be completely detached from it to let them really run with it. But, what would they do? I always have this curious about that, I would say. Not curious enough to find out, but still curious. It's always in the back of my head.
turns.zh:
我得说，过去几年里，我越来越常思考：“我还要坚持多久？”我一直在犹豫不决。我可以告诉你，有趣的是，现在的我比过去多年来都要兴奋。但一年前我可没这么激动。做这行久了，难免会拿早期和现在做比较——早期多么轻松，现如今却困难重重。是喜欢这种挑战，还是宁愿另辟蹊径？这些回忆如潮水般涌来，我会怀念过去，也会畅想未来。（00:23:16）：“是啊，我们20个人的时候可轻松多了。”“没错，但那时根本没这般压力，而且时代不同了，回不去了。”不过有意思的是，明年我就50岁了，我们做这行也25年了。经营这家公司25年，我有时会想：“够了吗？”但此刻，我对我们正在做的事充满热情。我们正在开发一些极棒的产品，可能是近年来最出色的作品。即将推出名为ONCE的新品类，明年我们计划在此基础上再开发三款产品。我还想再写本书，终于又有了新思路。（00:23:53）：现在真是精力充沛。我特别注意保持这种热情。如今，业务本身就是能量来源。过去有段时间，业务反倒成了消耗精力的黑洞。一旦精力被过度消耗，你就会怀疑：“这值得吗？还要继续吗？”但现在我又被激情点燃了。但一年后情况会怎样？真说不准。做这行越久，越容易审视自己。

（00:24:21）：还有个奇怪的幻想：我总好奇别人会怎么经营这家公司？如果明天有别人接手，他们会怎么做？除了我，从来没人有机会真正运营它。他们会做出哪些不同之处？要做到完全放手才可能让他们自由发挥。但他们会怎么做？我对此总是充满好奇，虽然没到非要一探究竟的程度，但好奇心始终萦绕心头。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think they'd do?
turns.zh: 你觉得他们会怎么做？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I think they'd probably be focused on growth. I think there's opportunities that we miss all the time. I think that we are stuck in a certain... Stuck sounds like a negative term, but I don't mean it that way. But, we're stuck in a certain groove. We do things the way we do things. We change the way we do things here and there, but we're not really jumping into a new groove. I think someone would jump into a new groove and run the company differently, maybe make a lot more products than we're making today. Maybe resurrect a couple of things that we did in the past. Probably spend a lot on advertising, a lot of marketing, probably take our margin way down and try to focus on growth. What if we spent 70% of our margin on growth? What would that look like? I just feel like that's what most people would probably come in with a business like ours and do. They go, "Oh my god, there's so many missed opportunities here. Look at this, and look at this, and look at this. You've got this brand, and people know about you, and you've got 100,000 paying customers. Think about all the things you could do." I'm not really thinking about all the things we could do. I'm thinking about what we're doing. So I think someone else would come in and think about the things we could do. (00:25:49): I'm thinking about the things we are doing, with a little bit of a look ahead to things we could also do, but they're still pretty close to what we're doing today. So, that's what I think would happen. It'd be interesting. It'd be neat to live in a reality where there could be a second reality running right alongside you, truly. Not an A/B test, which is hard to do. You can't really A/B test an entire company. I'd seek to A/B test small things. But, it'd be cool if that was something that could happen. Maybe there's some simulation down the road.
turns.zh: 我觉得他们很可能专注于增长。我认为我们总是错过很多机会。我觉得我们被困在某种……“被困”听起来是个负面词汇，但我不是这个意思。不过，我们确实陷入了一种惯性思维模式。我们做事的方式一成不变，偶尔会调整一下策略，但从根本上来说，我们并没有真正跳出固有思维框架。我觉得如果有人接手我们的公司，他们会采取全新的运营方式，也许会生产比现在更多的产品，甚至重启一些过去的项目。他们很可能会大力投放广告、加强营销，降低利润率以专注于增长。假如我们把70%的利润率用于增长会怎样？那会是个什么样的局面？我觉得大多数人接手我们这样的公司都会这么做。他们会惊呼：“天哪，这里有太多错失的机会了。看看这个，看看那个，看看这个。你拥有这个品牌，人们都知道你，还有10万名付费用户。想想你能做多少事啊。”但我并没有真正去思考我们能做什么。我只在思考我们正在做的事。所以我觉得如果有其他人接手，他们会考虑我们能做的事。（00:25:49）：我现在思考我们正在做的事，同时也会展望未来可能能做的事，但这些都和我们现在做的事非常相似。所以我觉得如果有人接手会是这样。这会很有趣。如果能在现实中同时运行另一个平行世界，那就太棒了。但这很难做到，你没法对整个公司进行A/B测试。我可能会对一些小细节进行A/B测试。但如果真能实现那种情况，那就太棒了。也许未来会有某种模拟环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just thinking-
turns.zh: 我只是在想——

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: It's a possibility.
turns.zh: 这是有可能的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe we're in the simulation variant where you're still running it.
turns.zh: 也许我们正处于模拟版本中，人们还在按照既定模式运营。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: It could be.
turns.zh: 这也有可能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's another... This a cool exercise, actually, just to think about it. If I were to bring in any leader, what would they do? Just as a thought exercise.
turns.zh: 还有另一种……其实这是一个很有趣的思考练习。如果我引入任何一位领导者，他们会怎么做？就当是个思维实验。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: This is a weird way to think about it, but I almost would be embarrassed by what someone would come in and look at, and go, "Oh my God, you guys are missing so many opportunities here." I'd be like, "Yeah, I know. I know we are, but I'm totally fine with it." But, there'd be this moment of judgment and reckoning with, "Do you realize how much you're leaving on the table?" You could have five different pricing tiers, and make a lot more money, and you can maximize this and maximize that, and squeeze this and squeeze that, and address this market, and you could have special versions of Basecamp. Wow, churches are using Basecamp? We could do a special version for churches, and for synagogues, and religious institutions, or education or nonprofits. Think of all the slight different things you could do with these different..." (00:27:06): I'm certain that all those opportunities exist on the table. They don't interest me, personally, in terms of making multiple products. But I could see someone else going, "There's a huge opportunity here. We got to pursue this." I'd be really proud if someone did that, and made the business bigger and better. I could never have done that. I'm glad someone else did that. But right now, we're running it our way.
turns.zh: 这么想挺奇怪的，但要是有人进来一看，说：“天哪，你们这儿真是错失了太多机会。”我可能会回应：“是啊，我知道。但我完全没关系。”不过，肯定会有人批评你：“你知道自己错过了多少潜在收益吗？”你本可以设定五个不同的定价层级，多赚不少钱，还能优化这优化那，开发针对特定市场的版本，甚至推出Basecamp的定制版本。哇，教堂都在用Basecamp？我们可以为教堂、犹太教堂、宗教机构、教育机构或非营利组织开发专属版本。想想还有哪些细微的改进空间……（00:27:06）：我确信这些机会都摆在眼前。但就我个人而言，我对开发多款产品没什么兴趣。不过我能想象有人会说：“这儿有巨大机遇，我们必须抓住它。”如果真有人这么做，让公司发展得更大更好，我会由衷感到骄傲。我自己永远做不到这点。但目前，我们还是按照自己的方式经营。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to this as a path people can take with their business versus a traditional venture scale business, this path is essentially build something, sell it, make money, live like a chill life. Not super stressed, growth-focused obsessed, need to build a billion-dollar company. Do you think this path is something everyone should do? Is it a specific type of personality, a specific type of product? Do you recommend people that sometimes do go this big shot venture scale route?
turns.zh: 回到人们可以选择的创业路径，与传统的大规模风险投资型企业相比，这条路本质上就是先做成产品、卖出去、赚钱，然后享受轻松生活。无需承受巨大压力，痴迷于增长速度，非要打造价值数十亿美元的公司不可。你觉得这条路适合所有人吗？它是否需要特定类型的人格或特定类型的产品？对于那些偶尔选择大规模风险投资路径的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I'm glad there are some people who do that. I'm glad that there's some businesses that-
turns.zh: 我很高兴有人能做到这些。我很高兴有些企业——

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: People who do that. I'm glad that there's some businesses that wouldn't have worked out had they not taken a bunch of funding and went big, clearly. And there's many impressive businesses that do that. But let's face it, those are extreme outliers. The majority of companies on this planet run like ours. They're bootstrapped, they don't have any money. No one's willing to give them a penny and they open up a shop somewhere, they do something, they put their shingle out and they launch a website or whatever and they try to make it work. So most people are doing it our way, even though in our industry it seems like we're the outliers, but we're not. We're actually incredibly boring and mainstream, really. If you were to pick any random business owner on the street, they'd run their business like us. I got to make more money than I spend otherwise I'm out. I don't have this big cushion of millions sitting in the bank that I can just spend on things. (00:28:48): So they're pretty, they keep an eye on costs. They think about this carefully. But yeah, I'm glad there's people who are going for the moonshot and doing it their way and doing it a different way. And the world moves forward sometimes because of those businesses and it's great. It's great and I admire them. It's just that it's not the path I would take and I think because that's not who I am, and I think this is the important point that I want to get across, is I'm not really, hopefully I don't come off as encouraging everyone to be like me. I'm not saying that at all. What I'm saying is this is a way to be. It's an alternative to what you're often hearing in our industry, which is like go big or go home, raise a bunch of money and get huge and unicorn status and the whole thing. (00:29:29): That's a way. Just know though that basically almost nobody makes it that way. Really, almost nobody really makes it that way. And there's a lot more room to make it and to build a successful business, if you throw out that outlier and look at all the other places you can land as a business. So my interest is optionality. If I could land in 135 different positions and have a sustainable business, that's great. Versus saying there's only one way I'm going to be successful or happy. Those odds aren't really in anyone's favor. Even though of course some people win the lottery. And I'm not saying it's luck. There is luck, a lot of luck, including we're lucky that we've made it. So there is a degree of that when I say lottery. But really the point is that there's only a few slots for a few companies like that at any one time. Meanwhile, there are hundreds or thousands of slots for other kinds of companies to make it if they don't go for the moon.
turns.zh: 那些做事的人。很高兴看到有些企业如果没有获得大量资金并大举扩张，可能就无法成功，这显然是事实。也有许多令人钦佩的企业采取了这种策略。但说实话，这些都是极端的个例。地球上的大多数公司都像我们这样经营——自力更生，没有资金支持。没人愿意给他们一分钱，他们只能在某个地方开店、开展业务、挂出招牌、建立网站，然后努力让它运转起来。大多数人都在按照我们的方式做事，即便在我们这个行业里，人们似乎认为我们才是异类，但事实并非如此。我们其实非常普通、非常主流。随便在街上挑一个企业主，他们的经营方式都和我们类似。我必须赚得比花得多，不然就出局了。我没有银行里存着数百万美元随时可以挥霍的巨额资金。（00:28:48）：所以他们很精明，密切关注成本，深思熟虑每一步。但说真的，我很高兴有一些人敢于追逐宏伟目标，用自己的方式另辟蹊径。世界有时正因这些企业而进步，这很棒，我很钦佩他们。但这不是我会选择的道路，因为这不符合我的性格。我想强调的关键点是，我不是在鼓励大家效仿我。我只是想说，这是一种可行的经营方式。与我们行业常听到的“要么大干一场，要么出局”，要么筹集大量资金、迅速壮大、成为独角兽企业等说法不同，（00:29:29）：这是一种选择。只要你抛开那些极端案例，审视其他成功的可能性，就会有更大的成功空间。所以我的关注点在于选择权。如果我能在135种不同位置立足并维持可持续的业务，那就太棒了。而不是说只有一种成功或快乐的路径。这种概率对任何人都不利。当然，有些人中了彩票，我不是说这全靠运气。虽然运气很重要，包括我们能成功也是运气的结果。所以我说彩票的时候确实有运气的成分。但关键是，任何时候能达到这种规模的公司都屈指可数。与此同时，如果其他类型的公司不追求极致目标，成功的机会却成千上万。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to close this thought around whether, if you have an idea going the venture route makes sense. What do venture scale companies need to achieve? What investors look for that to even work out? To your point, it almost never works out. What is it you have to do for it to feel like, okay, this is a venture scale idea versus this is an awesome idea. We could just make money every year, every month from it and not raise money and life will be great.
turns.zh: 最后再总结一下关于是否该走风险投资路线的思考。风险投资级别的公司需要达到什么标准才能成功？投资者看重哪些条件才能让这件事可行？正如你所说，几乎从未成功过。那么你需要做些什么才能判断这是一个风险投资级别的想法，而不是一个很棒的想法？我们每年、每月都能从中获利，不需要融资，生活也会很美好。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I'm probably the wrong person to ask, but I would say there are versions of our... Let's just take Monday for example. Basecamp and Monday are quite a bit different, but they live in the same world. We could have flipped, someone could have had the Monday approach and sold Basecamp that way, and Basecamp could have gone big in that way and Monday could have stayed small in our way. Again, I'd rather be my business than their business. I would not trade Basecamp for Monday's business any day of the week because I love what we're doing. We're profitable, we're happy. We don't have to deal with the things they have to deal with. So I wouldn't trade businesses or places with anybody. But you could imagine it could have been swapped. So it's not that Basecamp couldn't be this big venture scale, whatever you want to call it, although look, hey, we have the same number of customers roughly than they do. (00:31:46): Are we? I guess we are venture scale in that respect. But again, point is is that depending on how you approach it, you can take anything in any different direction. So it's more of a mindset, what are you after? We're not after that and they are. So that's what they do. And we do it a different way. So I don't necessarily think... There's things like Airbnb is a great example that that has to have a certain degree of scale to really be something that no matter where you go in the world, you're like, I can get an Airbnb there. And that's probably going to take money to get there. Same thing with Uber. Uber's another example, and these are easy to pick, but they're great examples really. When Uber was getting started and they had to proliferate all over the country to begin with and all over the world. (00:32:33): So it was this reliable thing you could think of just you would think of a cab. If I went to New York or Chicago, I knew there'd be a cab. Was there going to be an Uber? I don't know. Well, you have to know that there's going to be one to begin to trust us. So in order to do that, you have to expand rapidly. So there's that kid of, those kind of businesses exist and those are great examples of venture-backed companies that kind of need that massive initial push to be available in all the different places because they're actual physical products. Airbnb's a physical product, Uber's a physical product, Basecamp, Monday, Asana, they're available everywhere instantly anyway. I don't know what you need the money for other than marketing. And it's interesting because marketing's losing them a lot of money. So it's an interesting thing. But anyway, you can talk to them about that.
turns.zh: 我可能不是合适的回答者，但我会说我们的产品版本……以Monday为例。Basecamp和Monday有很大的不同，但它们身处同一个生态圈。我们本可以调整策略，采用Monday的模式来出售Basecamp，或许Basecamp也能因此壮大，而Monday则保持小规模运营。再说一次，我宁愿经营自己的业务，也不愿接手别人的公司。无论何时，我都不会用Basecamp换取Monday的业务，因为我热爱我们正在做的事。我们盈利了，员工快乐，也无需应对他们必须应对的种种挑战。所以我不会与任何人交换业务或团队。但你可以想象这种局面本可能发生。因此，Basecamp并非无法发展成大型企业——无论你如何定义规模，尽管看看吧，我们的客户数量与他们大致相当。（00:31:46）：我们是吗？从这个角度看，我们确实具备了企业规模。但关键在于，你如何看待这件事？我们不追求那种规模，而他们却在追逐。这就是他们的策略。我们采取了不同的方法。所以我不认为……Airbnb就是一个很好的例子，它必须达到一定的规模才能真正做到无论你身处世界何处，都能找到Airbnb房源。这很可能需要大量资金投入。Uber也是如此。Uber初期必须在全美乃至全球范围内扩张。（00:32:33）：它必须像出租车一样可靠。如果我去纽约或芝加哥，就知道能叫到出租车。但Uber呢？谁知道呢？不过用户得先相信Uber的存在才能使用。因此，Uber必须快速扩张。这种类型的企业确实存在，它们是典型的风投支持的公司，需要初期的大规模推广才能在全球范围内普及，因为它们是实体产品。Airbnb是实体产品，Uber也是实体产品，而Basecamp、Monday、Asana等产品本质上是即时可用的服务。除了营销之外，我不明白他们为什么需要资金。更有趣的是，营销反倒让他们亏损严重。这确实是个有趣的现象。不过你可以和他们聊聊这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to start chatting about your ways of working, how you operate at 37signals. There's a lot of really unique approaches. One is you mentioned that every project is, I didn't know this. It's two people, a designer and engineer, and then two to six weeks of work. Can you just expand on how you actually do that, how broad development works there?
turns.zh: 我想先聊聊你们在37signals的工作方式。你们有很多独特的做法。比如你提到每个项目都由两人，一个设计师和工程师，共同完成，然后投入两到六周的时间。能否详细讲讲你们具体是如何运作的，开发流程是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah, so we have framework development framework we invented called Shape Up, and if you go to basecamp.com/shapeup, you can read the book, it's free. You can also get a print version if you want. Shape Up is our methodology for actually building products. And part of this is this idea at the root of it is this idea of the six-week cycle. That whatever we choose to do can take no longer than six weeks. So this is not an estimate of time, it's an appetite, which is a radically different approach. It doesn't sound like that much of a different word, but it really is. An estimate is like how long do we think it's going to take? And however long it takes is however long it takes. And most human beings are terrible estimators. We all are pretty much terrible estimators. So that's why things keep going and going and going and going. (00:34:21): We instead have appetites. And our appetite for any individual feature is no more than six weeks. Essentially that's our budget we're willing to spend. I'm only willing to spend six weeks in any feature. So we have to figure out the simplest, most effective version of that to get that done within six weeks and get it done by two people. Now, not everything gets the full six weeks. Some things were like, we have a one week appetite for this. This is not that big of a deal. If we have it, great. If we don't have it, that's fine. We're willing to spend a week on it. Not that it could take a week, because it could also take 12 weeks if we give it 12 and it could take 24, if we give it 24. Work expands to fill the time available. So for us it's about appetite. (00:35:00): So the idea of appetites, maxing things out at six weeks, two people max, and then there's a lot of other details, and I could go on for an hour about Shape Up, people can read about it. But it's those fundamental principles, appetites, six week max, small teams and this idea of shaping the work ahead of time, then giving the team a lot of latitude to figure out how to get that thing done. We don't have a spec, we don't create to-dos or tasks or tickets for people. They create the work that needs to get done to fulfill the idea that we've written up and designed essentially, and they figure out how to do it. Then we trade. So they might get into something that we've said, we have about six weeks. Well, we're only give it six weeks and two weeks in they go, we actually stumbled into something we didn't realize. (00:35:50): This is probably not going to be able to be done the way we thought. So can we do it this way? And then we have a discussion and there's a conversation. There's a lot of molding and changing that happens along that period of time. We call it trading concessions. There's all the trade-offs we're always thinking about. So all these things that come to bear. And then people often ask, well, what if you don't get it done in the six weeks you gave it? Well, so it depends. So in most cases it should die, meaning it just doesn't happen. Because if we say we're going to give it six weeks and we give it seven or eight or nine or 10, then we're not really giving it six weeks, we're giving it 10, then we don't really have a system. (00:36:27): There are times though, when there's a couple days left when we're on what we're calling the downslope. So we have these things in Basecamp called hill charts. And things that are on, that's actually work... A project's more like a hill. It's not like a linear line. If you're on the left side of the hill, it means you're still pushing this thing up the hill. You're still trying to figure out how to do this. But once work gets to the top, it's downhill from there. It's just pure execution and we know how to nail it. So if we're almost at the bottom of the hill on something and it needs two more days, fine. If there's any work that's left over that's still on the left side of the hill, meaning we're still pushing it up, we don't know how we're going to do it and we're at our time limit, it almost certainly dies. So there are some contextual decisions to make at that point, but fundamentally that's how we approach work. And this prevents long running projects that never end, which by the way are the most demoralizing kinds of projects. (00:37:17): Things that you're stuck on that you don't want to do that never end, sucks. And if people get stuck on a couple of those, they want to leave their job. So the implications here are significant. And so we want to keep people out of that zone of like, I hate this work and it goes on forever. Because sometimes you're going to hate the work. Not all projects are that exciting. Sometimes it's maintenance stuff, sometimes it's updating an internal billing system that's boring and no customers are going to see but needs to be done. But you'll know that, hey, at maximum we've got four weeks on this. I can already see the end from the beginning, no big deal. But if it's like this is going to take nine months and you're on week four and you're like, I hate this, bad. So we want to stay away from that sort of thing.
turns.zh:
是的，我们开发了一个叫做“Shape Up”的框架，如果你访问basecamp.com/shapeup，可以免费阅读相关书籍。如果你需要纸质版也可以获取。Shape Up是我们实际开发产品的方法论。其核心理念是六周周期法则——任何我们决定开发的功能，周期都不超过六周。这不是时间估算，而是欲望驱动——这两种思路截然不同。估算通常是“我们认为需要多长时间”，而欲望则是“我们最多愿意花费六周时间”。大多数人都是糟糕的估算师，所以项目总会拖延。

（00:34:21）我们转而用“欲望”来驱动开发。每个功能的欲望周期不超过六周，这就是我们愿意投入的预算。我只愿意在每个功能上花费六周时间。有些功能可能只需要一周完成，这没关系——有则锦上添花，无则无伤大雅。我们用一周时间去尝试。如果一周能完成，那就用一周；如果需要12周，那就12周。工作会根据可用时间自动调整。所以关键在于欲望。

（00:35:00）欲望驱动、六周周期、两人团队是核心原则。还有其他细节，我可以花一小时详细讲解Shape Up，但关键是这些基本原则：欲望驱动、六周周期、小组协作，以及提前规划工作的习惯。团队不需要依赖规格文档或任务列表，他们会自主完成设计任务，找到实现创意的路径。例如，如果我们原定六周完成，结果团队只用了两周，他们就会发现隐藏的价值，重新调整方案。

（00:35:50）人们常问：如果六周内完不成怎么办？这取决于具体情况。大多数情况下，项目会被终止，因为如果承诺六周却用了七八九十周，那就不是真正的六周周期了。但有时会在最后几天发现转机，比如项目进入下坡阶段（Basecamp中的“hill chart”）。左边的进度线代表爬坡阶段，右边的代表下坡阶段。
知道该怎么做。但一旦工作进入高峰阶段，接下来的路就越来越容易了。剩下的就是纯粹的执行，我们知道如何把它做好。所以如果我们在某个项目上几乎到了终点，还需要两天时间，那没关系。但如果还有工作堆积在山脚下，意味着我们还在往上爬，却又不知道怎么解决，并且已经到了时间限制，项目几乎注定失败。所以这时候就需要做出一些因地制宜的决策，但从根本上讲，这就是我们处理工作的方式。这样就能避免那些永远做不完的长期项目——顺便说一句，这种项目最容易让人泄气。（00:37:17）那些让你卡住、不想做、又永远做不完的工作，真是糟心透了。如果人们被困在这样的项目里，他们就会想辞职。所以这里的影响非常重大。因此，我们要让人们避免陷入那种"我讨厌这份工作，却还要一直做下去"的境地。因为有时候你确实会讨厌工作。不是所有项目都那么令人兴奋。有时是维护性的工作，有时是更新内部计费系统，既无聊又没客户会看到，但必须完成。但你要清楚，嘿，这个项目最多四周就能完成。我从一开始就能看到尽头，不算什么。但如果项目要花九个月，而你现在才第四周，却想"我讨厌这个"，那就糟糕了。所以我们要尽量避免这种情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have these quotes along these lines about planning, long-term business planning is a fantasy. I don't plan long-term because I want to do what I think, not what I thought.
turns.zh: 关于规划，长期商业规划不过是空想。我不做长期规划，因为我想做的是当下想做的事，而不是过去想做的事。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love these. This whole idea of appetites, it's very appealing. It makes so much sense. It's like the ultimate impact to effort calculation. The effort we'll put into this is fixed and we'll not go beyond this because the impact we expect from this is pretty clear. And if the effort goes up and up and up, well why did we even do this? But obviously the downside is you can't promise things really to sales marketing, which I think makes sense in your type of business. Do you see this work in businesses that aren't your business this approach?
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这些观点。这种关于欲望的理念太吸引人了，非常有道理。这就像是对努力投入的终极考量——我们投入的精力是固定的，不会超出预期，因为预期的回报是显而易见的。但如果投入的精力不断增加，那我们当初为什么还要做这件事呢？不过显然缺点是，你无法向销售和市场部门做出确切承诺。我觉得这在你这类业务中是合理的。你认为这种方法在非你所在的行业中也适用吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Well, let me talk about promises for a second. Promises are the downfall of every business. Every time we've made a promise to get something out in a certain period of time and we kind of inevitably seem to miss it, it's funny how it's almost like it would've been out in time, but the fact that we'd promised it made it not deliver in time. There's some strange thing that happens when you promise things. So we've learned to not promise anything. We can share what we're working on if we want to. We can tell people we're doing something. And by the way, the worst promise, and by the way, we've made a couple of these recently, we always regret them. It's like by the end of the year. That's the one promise you got to be very careful of, because it's so easy to make. There's nothing easier than promising work later. (00:39:29): And the further away it is, the easier it is to promise. And so this whole, by the end of the year, oh, red flag. Just remind yourself whenever you say that to yourself, go, oh, wait a second. Wait, wait, what am I doing right now? Because you're probably setting yourself up for disappointment. So as far as other companies running this way, there are a number of other companies that are running this way and more and more are adopting Shape Up all the time. But it's a struggle. It's hard. It's hard to change the way you work. I think companies form roots and roots go in the ground and once your root structure is formed, the plant that grows from that is the plant that grows from that, basically. You kind of have to uproot. And this is not really a totally clear metaphor because that plant is that plant, but you almost have to plant a new seed somewhere else, let's just say, and then grow something new because it's very hard to change in flight and change what you have and change what you're used to. (00:40:24): So what we often encourage people to do is keep working the way you're working, but some future project, some low criticality project, try this new method on that. So if it doesn't work, because it's probably not going to work very well the first time, just like if I gave you a guitar and you never played before, it'd be unreasonable for me to expect you to play well. You're going to suck for a while. So go pick some things that don't matter if you suck at them for a while and try this method over there and go, oh, you know what? I'm actually getting quite good. Now let's try to bring this into some more critical stuff. I think that's the important way to approach these sorts of projects, which is to take the criticality out. Because what ends up happening is that when people try to try something new on something really critical and it doesn't work, they'll never try it again. (00:41:08): They've destroyed all future opportunities to try this again, because everyone knows how bad it went last time on something that really mattered. And they would've gone, we could have done it our old way. Our old way worked. It kind of sucked, but it worked. And so now you're comparing two things that aren't really comparable, but you're always going to go with the momentum that you had versus the new thing. And so you got to be careful with that. So I know I'm rambling a bit on it, but that's my general sense and feel on how to adopt a different way of working.
turns.zh: 好吧，让我先谈谈承诺的问题。承诺是每个企业的致命弱点。每次我们承诺在某个时间段内完成某项任务时，几乎不可避免地会延期。奇怪的是，总觉得只要再坚持一下就能按时完成，但正是我们对承诺的执着导致了延期。当你承诺某件事时，总会出现一些奇怪的状况。所以我们学会了不轻易许诺。如果有想分享的进展，可以适时告知。如果想告知别人我们正在做某件事，那没问题。但最糟糕的承诺——说实话，我们最近就做过几次这种承诺，事后总会后悔。比如“年底前完成”这种承诺，尤其要谨慎，因为这种承诺太容易做出了。没有什么比承诺在未来某个时间点完成工作更容易的了。（00:39:29）而且承诺的期限越久远，越容易出问题。比如“年底前完成”，哦，危险信号。每当你对自己说这句话时，要提醒自己：等等，等等，我现在在做什么？因为你很可能正在为自己设下失望的陷阱。至于其他公司如何应对这种情况，有很多公司都在沿着这条路走，越来越多的公司在采用 Shape Up 方法。但这并不容易。改变工作方式很难。我认为公司会形成根深蒂固的习惯模式，一旦根基形成，发展出的植物也会受其限制。你得把根连根拔起。这不是一个完全贴切的比喻，因为原来的植物还是原来的植物，但你几乎得在别处重新播种，然后培育新的东西，因为在执行过程中做出改变、改变现有习惯和流程实在太难了。（00:40:24）所以我们通常鼓励人们继续保持现有工作方式，但在未来的某个项目上，某个低优先级的项目，可以尝试新方法。如果不成功——因为第一次尝试很可能效果不佳，就像如果我给你一把吉他，而你从未弹过吉他，指望你弹得好是荒谬的。你肯定会一开始很糟糕。所以选一些暂时失败也没关系的项目，在那里尝试新方法，然后发现：“哦，我其实已经做得不错了。”现在让我们把它应用到更关键的项目中。我认为这才是处理这类项目的正确方法——去除关键性。因为最终的结果是，当人们在真正关键的项目上尝试新方法却失败时，他们再也不会重试了。他们会毁掉未来再次尝试的机会，因为每个人都知道上次在真正重要的事情上失败得有多惨。他们会说：“我们本可以用老方法完成的。老方法虽然不完美，但至少能行。” 于是你会把两个根本不可比拟的东西放在一起比较，但你总会倾向于选择既有的惯性和新方法之间的平衡。所以在这方面要小心。我知道我讲得有点冗长，但这就是我对如何采用不同工作方式的总体看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's also this cool down period after one of these, what do you call these? A sprint or what's the term for it?
turns.zh: 还有这种冲刺阶段结束后的冷却期，该怎么称呼这种阶段呢？冲刺阶段还是别的术语？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: No, I hate that term. I don't like the word sprint because how do you feel after a sprint? Exhausted.
turns.zh: 是的，我讨厌这个词。我不喜欢“冲刺”这个词，因为冲刺之后你会有什么感觉？筋疲力尽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But also pretty good.
turns.zh: 但其实也挺好的。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: You can. Yeah, yeah. It's funny because I was a sprinter in high school, so I love sprinting. But if you go all out, you might feel high for a minute, but you can't go all out again. You've got to really catch your breath and you certainly like to sprint. I remember my track coach actually ran in college for a year until I realized that I wasn't good enough. But he made us run 20 200s in a row with just two minutes break in between, and the 200 is an incredibly hard race. You're all out for 200 meters or yards. And after the fifth one I just threw up. I just threw up. It's like that's kind of what work is for a lot of people. It's like 20 200s, they have these sprints and they never seem to end. And there's one sprint after the other, after the other, after the other, after the other. (00:42:36): And that's why I don't like the word because you can't layer that back to back to back to back. You cannot sprint back to back, to back, to back in life. And you can't do it at work. People do it at work, but I don't think it actually works. So what we do is after our six week cycles, we typically take what we call a two-week cool down. So we call these cycles, not sprints. A two-week cool down, and we call them cycles because cycles happen again and again and again. Sprints start and end. Cycles happen. There's cycles in life and seasons, and I like that idea that you're prepared for this thing to happen again. (00:43:12): Take two weeks, cool down. That's when people can sort of internally freelance. They're still working, but they're kind of tightening up a couple of things. Maybe we just shipped or working on a couple extra days on something that didn't ship that's going to ship in two days, or kind of fixing some bugs and messing around with some stuff that they wanted to get to, but no one ever had time to and was never scheduled. So that's kind a good time to do that. In the meantime, a few of us are shaping up the next cycles projects and finalizing that and writing the pitches up for that. So that's what those cycles are for. It's not that you're stopping work, it's that you're doing other kinds of work. And that I think is replenishing and refreshing, and I think that's the important part versus back to back to back sprints of the same kind of work all the time.
turns.zh: 你可以的。对，对。这挺有趣的，我高中时就是个短跑运动员，所以我喜欢冲刺。但如果你全力以赴，可能会兴奋一阵子，但你没法一直保持这种状态。你得真正喘口气。不过你确实喜欢冲刺。我记得我的田径教练在大学时跑了一年，直到我意识到自己不够出色。但他让我们连续跑20组200米，中间只有两分钟休息，而200米比赛极其艰苦。你要全力冲刺200米或码。跑到第五组时，我直接吐了。我真的吐了。这就像很多人的工作状态。就像一连串的冲刺，似乎永无止境。一个接一个，接一个，接一个，接一个。（00:42:36）：这就是我不喜欢这个词的原因，因为你没法连续不断地这样做。生活中没法连续不断地冲刺。工作中人们也这样做，但我觉得这根本没用。所以我们每完成六周的周期后，通常会进入为期两周的冷却期。我们把这些周期称为冷却期，而不是冲刺期。冷却期持续两周，我们称之为周期，因为周期会一次又一次地重复。冲刺有起有止，周期则持续不断。生活中有周期，有四季的更迭。我喜欢这种为下一轮周期做好准备的理念。（00:43:12）：休息两周，冷却一下。这段时间人们可以内部自由发挥。他们还在工作，但会调整一些事情。可能刚完成某个项目，又赶上某个未完成的项目要在两天内上线，或者修补一些漏洞，处理一些一直想做但没时间、没排上日程的小事。总之，这是个不错的时机。与此同时，我们中有些人会筹备下一个周期的项目，敲定方案，撰写提案。这就是周期存在的意义。不是停止工作，而是转换到其他工作模式。我觉得这能让人恢复精力、获得灵感，这才是关键所在，而不是一直重复同一种冲刺式的工作，没完没了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned also that you have no growth goals, that you make decisions a lot on instinct and gut and opinion, which sounds amazing, it's great if you could pull it off. Feels also very hard to operationalize and maybe make the best decisions in times. Can you just talk about how you actually operationalize that and what you find happens when you approach things that way?
turns.zh: 你还提到自己没有成长目标，更多依赖直觉、本能和意见来做决策。这听起来很棒，如果能做到确实很棒。但要把这转化为可操作的流程，及时做出最佳决策，可能很难。你能谈谈如何将其付诸实践，以及这样做时会产生什么效果吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I'll just admit that that's the only way I've ever known how to work. I don't know how to make decisions by numbers or I don't find any joy in it, frankly. I've always been intuition driven and gut driven. And frankly, to be honest, I think everyone actually is. And this is part of the thing I want to write up. I've been thinking about writing about this. I think everything's a judgment call. And so yeah, data can play a part. All sorts of things can play a part, but unless you're letting a machine make the decision, that's purely rational. If you're asking a human to make it's a judgment call. They're bringing to bear thousands of things they know and don't know about that influence them about this particular decision. And it's why when companies hire executives, what are they looking for in executive? They typically go judgment and experience. (00:45:06): They're not like they can read an Excel spreadsheet. That's not the thing that matters. Anyone can read that or anyone can read a chart or you can learn to do that. They're looking for judgment and experience, which is a very amorphous thing. It's like, what is it really? Well, they've been around, they've seen a lot of things, they've absorbed a lot of experiences and they're going to bring those undescribable things to bear to make decisions for the business. So out of all the things, data might be one thing, but there's thousands of things that go into a decision that many of which you don't even know. And I just feel like I'm comfortable admitting that that I don't really know why I'm making these calls, but I'm making these calls regardless. And I'm not looking at a number and going, if this is fifty-one percent versus forty-nine, I'm going this way for sure. (00:46:01): That could be an input perhaps, but it's not the only input. And I think people should recognize that even if you're a data-driven person, there's so much more at play here. So I just feel like just being honest about that and that's sort of how I've always looked at it. And I also will admit, as I just mentioned, I don't know the things that go into my decision-making process, but I'm absolutely fascinated by decision-making. I think it's one of the most interesting human endeavors. And I would just say that give your intuition credit. Give your gut credit. It's absorbed everything. And plus the things that you don't know it absorbed that are valuable.
turns.zh: 我得承认，这是我唯一熟悉的工作方式。说实话，我不擅长用数据做决策，也从中找不到乐趣。我向来凭直觉和直觉行事。说真的，我觉得每个人都是如此。这也是我想写下来的部分之一。我一直在思考写这方面的内容。我认为一切都是判断的问题。数据当然可以发挥作用，但除非你让机器来做决定，否则这纯粹是理性的。如果你让一个人来做决定，那就是判断了。他们会综合考虑成千上万的已知和未知因素，这些因素都会影响他们的判断。这就是为什么公司招聘高管时，他们看重什么呢？他们通常看重判断力和经验。（00:45:06）：他们不要求你能读懂Excel表格。这不是关键。任何人都能读懂表格，任何人都能看懂图表，你也可以学会这些。他们看重的是判断力和经验，而这是一件很难界定的东西。比如说，这到底是什么？嗯，他们阅历丰富，见多识广，积累了大量经验，他们会运用这些难以言喻的因素为企业做决策。所以在所有因素中，数据可能是其中之一，但做决策还需要考虑成千上万的因素，其中很多你甚至都不知道。我坦然承认，我确实不知道自己为什么会做出这些判断，但无论如何我都会做出判断。我不会看着一个数字说，如果这是51%对49%，那我肯定会选择前者。这可能是一个参考因素，但绝不是唯一的参考因素。我认为人们应该认识到，即便你是一个数据驱动型的人，这里还有更多因素在起作用。所以我觉得坦诚面对这一点很重要，这也是我一直以来的看法。我也承认，正如我刚才提到的，我不知道自己的决策过程包含哪些因素，但我对决策过程深感着迷。我认为这是人类最有趣的活动之一。我只想说，要重视你的直觉，重视你的直觉判断。它吸收了所有信息。还有那些你不知道它吸收了的信息，也同样有价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's easier to do that if you're the founder running the company, obviously. Is there something you find that you can do to help your teammates approach things that way too? Do you just trust their instincts also in a similar way?
turns.zh: 如果你是一家公司的创始人兼CEO，那显然更容易做到这一点。有没有什么方法可以帮助你的团队成员也这样做呢？你是否也会以类似的方式信任他们的直觉？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah, you're right by the way, it is easy for me to sit up here and say this, I own the place. No one can fire me. I get it, right. I can be wrong all the time, go, my gut just told me to do this. And I understand, I do. I'm self-aware enough to understand that. But I think that by demonstrating that's how we make decisions, it creates space for other people to make decisions that way. And when we have conversations, I'm talking with my team about something, I'll often go, I don't really know. It feels like this. It feels this way. And they'll say, I feel this way. And I'll ask them, how do you feel? How do you feel? What we ask people in general is we say, what do you think? We don't say, what do you know? We often say, what do you think? We might say, what do you know? (00:47:43): But we also say, what do you think more time. And what does that mean? What do you think is, I don't know where these thoughts come from and I don't know what forms them. So I think it's interesting to look at the things we say and go, we actually do want people to think. And so I'll often say, what do you think or what do you feel or how does this feel? Is something we talk more about at work than pretty much anything else, which is like, how does this screen feel? How does this flow feel? How does this feature feel? How does this word feel? How does this sentence feel? How does this paragraph feel? How does this website feel? How does these colors feel? Because human beings feel. (00:48:20): And while we have a logical side to us and a rational side to us, we're primarily feeling creatures. Even if we don't admit it, we are. And so I'm always curious about that. So I bring that up a lot and I ask other people how they feel, and I think hopefully that encourages people to share that side of their opinion. And we almost never, sometimes we look at numbers to sort of be an input, but it's never prove that. I'll never say justify that. That's just not terminology or lingo that we ever bring up. It's not a way. (00:49:05): It's, how do you feel? It's not like, how certain are you? I try to tend to shy away from anything that's about certainty. We're not after certainty. I want to know how you think it feels. So anyway, I'm rambling again, but this is, I'm rambling because this is actually how things go. When we talk, there is a lot of this, it's not precise in a sense. It eventually becomes precise when it's out in the world, but the thought process is very rambling and very amorphous, and you kind of find your way as you go. And eventually go yeah, yeah, that's it. That's it. That feels right.
turns.zh: 是啊，你说得对。顺便说一句，我坐在这儿说这些话确实容易，因为这地方是我的。没人能解雇我。我懂的，对吧。我可以一直犯错，随便吧，我的直觉告诉我该这么做。我明白的，我确实明白。我足够自知，明白这一点。但我认为，通过展示我们就是这样做决定的方式，就为其他人创造了这样做决定的空间。当我们开会时，我和团队讨论某个问题，我会经常说：我其实也不确定。感觉是这样。感觉是这样的。他们会说：我也这么觉得。我会问他们：你怎么想的？你怎么想的？我们对人们普遍的要求是，我们会说：你怎么看？我们不会说：你知道什么？我们可能也会说：你怎么看？但我们更多时候会说：你怎么想？这意味着什么？你怎么想就是说，我不知道这些想法从何而来，也不知道是什么塑造了它们。所以我觉得，审视我们说的话很有意思。比如，我们会说：你怎么想？你怎么感觉？这感觉如何？在工作中，我们谈论最多的，莫过于：这个界面感觉如何？这个流程感觉如何？这个功能感觉如何？这个词感觉如何？这个句子感觉如何？这个段落感觉如何？这个网站感觉如何？这些颜色感觉如何？因为人类是有感觉的。（00:47:43）虽然我们有逻辑的一面和理性的一面，但我们本质上是感性的。即使我们不承认，我们也是。于是我对此总是很好奇。所以我经常问别人你们怎么想，我想希望这能鼓励人们分享他们观点的这一面。几乎从不，我们有时会看看数据作为参考，但那绝不是证明。我绝不会说这是合理化。这不是我们提到的术语或行话。这不是方法。（00:49:05）而是，你怎么想的？不是你有多确定。我尽量避免任何关于确定性的话题。我们不追求确定性。我想知道你觉得这感觉如何。所以说，我又在东拉西扯了，但这就是实际情况。在我们交谈时，很多时候都是这样的，没有什么精确的。当想法付诸实践时，最终会变得精确，但思考过程是漫无边际、模糊不清的，你只能边走边找方向。最终你会说：对，对，就是这样。就是这样。感觉对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This kind of advice comes up a lot actually on this podcast, especially for product managers, that there's a lot of power in just trusting your instincts and not just being this kind of unbiased participant in a product team, having actual, here's what I think works from your own experience using the product from your own life experience. But this came up with Brian [inaudible 00:50:05] episode. He's running the company, he's telling everyone basically, here's what we're building. A lot of people said, okay, that'd be great if our CEO is also a designer, very product-minded person. Many people aren't that, many people don't have actual enough experience to have built amazing instincts. So, do you solve that by just hiring people that have a lot of experience? Is it like a hiring thing? Is it trust people that have a lot more experience more because not everyone's going to have the right instinct?
turns.zh: 实际上，在这个播客中，我们经常会听到这样的建议，特别是针对产品经理而言：相信自己的直觉至关重要，而不应只是产品团队中不偏不倚的参与者。更重要的是，要从自身使用产品的经验和生活经历中总结出有效的见解。但在布莱恩那期节目中，这个话题被提及。他作为公司CEO，基本上会告诉大家我们正在开发的产品。许多人表示，如果我们的CEO同时也是设计师、具备产品思维的人，那就太好了。但现实中很多CEO并非如此，他们往往缺乏足够的经验来培养出卓越的直觉能力。那么，解决这个问题的方法是招聘经验丰富的人吗？这是否关乎招聘策略？是否应该更信任经验更丰富的人呢？毕竟，并非每个人都能拥有正确的直觉。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: It's true. Look, Brian's probably one of the greatest CEOs around today, but I like small businesses. So he knows how to run a bigger organization. I wouldn't. So I can't really step into that answer from that perspective. One of the reasons we stay small, I think, is so we can all rub off on each other. And when we hire, we can be very, very selective because we only hire a few people a year. And so I only hire designers and product people, David hires programmers, and different people in the company hire different people. But when I hire designers, I'm curious about their tastes. I'm curious about what they like. I'm curious about what other products they think are good. I'm curious about what they've seen that they admire or who they... I'm always asking about that because that helps me get a sense of who they are and what lens they see the world through and what kind of influences they're going to bring to bear. So that's the kind of stuff I'm looking for. (00:51:34): And one of the things that we do during the interview process for designers specifically and product people, which is the same thing in my mind, is they do a project for us at the end. So the last five finalists will do a project for us. We'll pay them to do the project, they'll have a week to do it, they'll do it, and then I'll critique it with them. Even if I love it, I will push back in certain areas. And one of the things I'll often ask is, if you had another couple days, what would you do with this? And I want to see where people go with that. To me, that is where you can see they don't have any time to think. So where does their gut go? What are their instincts? Where do they arrive after having to riff on the spot with something? (00:52:18): So what's behind what they built? Because what they built should just be some of what they had in mind. It shouldn't be everything. Now they're exhausted of every future idea. And I've seen some people who we thought were really good, and in that moment, they don't know where to go with it. Now, that's not to say some people don't need time to think and think it through, but I'm still looking for people who just, their gut is filled with ideas. And so it doesn't always translate but that's how I try to suss out whether or not someone has a good gut instinct on where to go. And it almost doesn't necessarily even matter where they go with it because this is raw, just raw gut. But I want to see that they have one and they're willing to lean into it and not be afraid of saying things that may not make any sense. (00:53:08): But yeah, I've got some other ideas and we could try this, and we try this, and I kind of play with this idea. And I don't know. Actually, now that I'm thinking about it, maybe we try, what if we did that? What about this? And then I would say something and we'd riff and we start riffing. And when we start riffing, there's a synchronicity that I'm looking for. And when I feel that synchronicity and that resonance, the two wavelengths are just perfectly vibrating together, then I know we have something. So that's the kind of stuff I'm looking for when I hire people. And I do think that that translates to people with a better gut feel than someone who's more of a, let's call it an academic product person, which can be very fine at other places, but it wouldn't really work here.
turns.zh:
确实如此。听着,布莱恩或许是当今最出色的CEO之一,但我更喜欢小型企业。所以他知道如何运营大型组织,而我做不到。因此我无法从这个角度来评价他。我认为我们保持公司规模小的原因之一,就是让大家能相互启发。在招聘员工时,我们可以非常挑剔,因为我们每年只招聘少数人。所以我只招设计师和产品人员,大卫招程序员,公司不同部门也有各自的招聘标准。但在招聘设计师时,我会关注他们的审美品味,喜欢什么样的产品,欣赏哪些设计作品,或者欣赏谁的作品。这些都是我感兴趣的问题,因为这能让我了解他们的个性和思维方式,以及他们会带来怎样的影响力。这就是我所寻求的。  

（00:51:34）:  在面试设计师和产品人员时(在我看来两者是一样的),我们会让他们为我们做一个项目。最后五名入围者会为我们做项目。我们会付钱给他们,给他们一周时间完成项目,然后我会和他们一起点评。即使我很喜欢他们的作品,也会在某些方面提出改进意见。我常问的一个问题是,如果再给你几天时间,你会怎么做?我想看看他们能在此基础上拓展到哪里。对我来说,这是判断他们是否有时间思考的机会。看看他们的直觉能带他们走向何方?在即兴发挥时,他们会产生怎样的灵感?  

（00:52:18）: 那么他们的作品背后隐藏着什么?因为他们的作品应该只是他们想法的一部分,不可能包含所有内容。现在他们已经耗尽了所有未来创意的可能。我见过一些我们认为很优秀的人,可在那一刻,他们却不知道该怎么做了。这并不是说有些人不需要时间思考和推敲,但我寻找的是那些直觉中充满想法的人。这种直觉不一定能完美转化,但我会试图判断他们是否有这样的直觉,是否愿意倾听并勇于表达那些看似不合逻辑的想法。  

（00:53:08）: 但我还有其他想法,我们可以尝试这个,再尝试那个。我会把这些想法玩味一番。我不知道。说实话,现在回想起来,或许我们可以试试看,如果我们这么做会怎样?这个怎么样?然后我会说出我的想法,我们开始即兴发挥。当即兴发挥开始时,会有一种共鸣感。我能感受到这种共鸣和共振,两者的波长完美同步,那我就知道我们找到了合适的方向。这就是我招聘时所看重的。我认为这比那些更偏向学术派的产品经理要好得多,后者在其他公司可能表现出色,但在这里行不通。

Because a lot of companies, a lot of leaders are like, we got plenty of ideas. We just need you to help us ship stuff.
turns.zh: 对我来说，对于那些寻求直觉敏锐、果断决策的人来说，这真是条绝佳建议。但有趣的是，这往往与大多数人的需求背道而驰——人们往往不希望对方只有满脑子的点子，因为很多公司和领导者都会说："我们有的是创意，就需要你帮我们把产品落地吧。"

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I don't want that either. So I don't want just ideas. So they have to make something that's clear. First of all, it has to be good and clear. And then they also have to be able to riff on the spot and think about how else they could take this. We've had some people who were just so scatterbrained and they've got a million ideas, but when we asked them to execute something for this project, it was a total mess. You could see their time management skills were off and they focused on the wrong things. That is not a go for me, that's a no go. (00:54:31): What's a go is that's a clever design, well executed, thoughtful, clear, and here's where they could take it from here on out if they had a few more days, or even if we had 15 minutes, what would you do you do with that? So that's the kind of stuff that I think ultimately is the meat of it. And so I always think of it in terms of play. This is play. I want to play with this product. I want to play with this design. I want to play with this idea. It's play and play is a thing. It's a very clear thing versus a rigid, boring approach to product development, which again, can be successful, but it wouldn't work at our company.
turns.zh: 我也不想要那种只会空想的人。他们必须拿出清晰的方案。首先，方案必须优秀且易于理解。然后，他们还得能即兴发挥，思考如何进一步优化。我们遇到过一些思路混乱、想法无数的人，但当我们让他们为项目执行任务时，结果却一团糟。他们的时间管理能力很差，重点也抓错了。这种人对我来说根本不行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you may have seen this question, but the question is, what is a spectacular failure of someone trying to follow your advice and failing when it doesn't stick? What is the reason?
turns.zh: 我想你可能已经看到这个问题了，但问题是：当有人试图遵循你的建议却失败时，会发生什么样的惨烈教训？原因是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: People trying to make a rapid, fundamentally, 180 degree changes quickly is a great way to fall flat on your face, basically. I have seen people who try to adopt, let's say, Shape Up, and they come back six weeks later and they're like, "This sucks. This doesn't work." I'm like, "I'm not surprised to hear that. Tell me how you did it." And then, they explain like, "Oh, the next project we did, we did this." I'm like, "Yeah, I'm really not surprised to hear that now." Because you can't really do that. You can't turn on a dime. There's this thing called momentum. I always try to think of things in terms of the physical world. The more massive an object, the more energy it takes to change its direction. This is why big companies move slowly. (00:57:26): This is also why momentum, which is the way you've been working for four years, is going to power you forward in a certain way. It's very hard to turn the corner immediately or turn around. You just cannot do it physically. If you can't do it physically, you can't do it this way. I think that's what I've seen, is these rapid like, "All right, starting tomorrow, we're starting Shape Up." It's like, well, no, it's not going to work. Unless you say we're going to do it on this other thing that doesn't matter so much. That's one thing I would say. (00:57:52): The other thing is that pretty much every business is a spectacular failure. It just is. It's like, business is really hard and the ones that make it are all outliers. This is why most businesses fail. There's a million reasons why, and it's always hard to pin it down. And we can all look back. By the way, I don't like to look back on things. I'm not much of a fan of looking back on failures and trying to figure out what went wrong so we don't do it again, because I don't think we know what went wrong. I think we can spend a long time trying to analyze it and we're going to find something that we can agree on, and it tends to be what you can agree on so you can move on. But that doesn't mean that's what it was. (00:58:37): Just like we don't really know why you make decisions, you don't really know why things didn't work. Sometimes there are some examples, and I think it's true if you're talking about a mechanistic system. You're stamping metal and it's supposed to have perfect circles and it's an oval. You can go back to that machine and see how the thing worked, and the line. You can adjust that and fix that. A lot of work though is not that way, especially software work, where there's a million different inputs and a million different people. It's not simple stamping machines. It's a different thing. I don't know, but I do think that trying to make big changes too quickly is a primary reason.
turns.zh: 试图迅速、彻底地做出180度大转变的人，往往会一败涂地。比如，我见过有人想采用“Shape Up”方法，结果六周后就回来抱怨：“这方法太烂了，根本不管用。”我会说：“这我一点都不惊讶。说说你具体是怎么做的。”结果他们会说：“哦，我们接下来的项目又换了新方向。”我会说：“嗯，听起来也不意外。”因为这根本行不通。改变方向绝非易事。这里有个叫“惯性”的概念。我总喜欢用现实世界的例子来解释：物体越重，改变其方向所需的能量就越大。这就是大公司行动迟缓的原因。（00:57:26）同样，四年来一直沿用的“惯性”模式也会以某种方式推动你前进。想要立即转向或掉头实在太难了。这在物理层面就是做不到的。如果现实层面做不到，策略层面也同样行不通。我观察到很多所谓的“快速转型”案例，比如“明天就开始用Shape Up”之类的。但结果往往不尽如人意。除非你先尝试一个无关紧要的项目作为过渡。（00:57:52）还有一点，几乎所有企业都是巨大的失败案例。这是事实。创业本就艰难，成功者都是异类。这就是大多数企业失败的原因。失败原因千千万万，总结起来却很难。回头看当然容易，但我不爱回顾失败。我不喜欢追究原因，因为即使找到症结，往往也是显而易见的部分，而非真正的原因。（00:58:37）就像我们不清楚自己为何做决定，也不明白为何事情会失败。有时能找到例子，比如机械系统出错——比如冲压金属本应是圆形，结果却成了椭圆形。你可以回溯流程，调整参数。但多数工作并非如此，尤其是在软件领域，存在无数输入变量和参与者。它不是机械冲压，而是复杂得多的系统。我不确定，但我确实认为急于做出重大变革是主要原因。

Maybe it's just simply the six-week cycle thing is the thing and the rest of it doesn't matter so much. Or it could be this idea of appetites versus estimates, and they can work that into the way they work. Take whatever works. You don't have to go wholesale on any of these things.
turns.zh: 是的，通常都是小团队。这和Airbnb的情况不同，布莱恩不会直接说：“好的，明天我们就按37signals团队提出的方案来做。” 但通常是大公司内部的小团队会尝试这种做法。有时这种做法能推广开来，有时则不然，而且也不一定非要推广。可能只是某个部门、某个团队采用不同的工作方式。（00:59:45）  此外，不一定要完全照搬Shape Up模式。可以只借鉴其中的30%。比如，六周迭代周期这个核心理念可能值得保留，其他部分则不必拘泥。又比如，关于“用户需求与预估”的理念，他们可以将其融入自己的工作流程。只要有用的东西都可以借鉴，不必全盘接受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. A second question comes from Leo Polovets, one of my favorite VCs. He works at Susa Ventures. He asked the question a lot of people actually asked. It's just, what does he think he got right and where has he changed his mind, if anywhere? You share a lot of strong opinions, very contrarian opinions. So, maybe just mostly on that second part is what I'm most curious about. What have you changed your mind about?
turns.zh: 太棒了。接下来是Leo Polovets的提问，他是我最喜欢的风投之一，供职于Susa Ventures。他提出了一个很多人都好奇的问题：他认为自己哪些做法是正确的，又有哪些地方改变了主意？你分享了很多强硬观点，甚至有些逆向思维。所以，我最感兴趣的还是后半部分。你在哪些方面改变了看法？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: A few years, well, a handful of years ago, we used to make multiple products, and we went to just doing Basecamp. I thought I would be personally satisfied for the rest of my career, working on one thing and just making that thing the best it could possibly be. Essentially, working on one sculpture, and constantly tweaking it and chiseling it and just polishing it, and just making it better and better, and better, and better, and better. I still thoroughly enjoy working on Basecamp. But a few years ago, we built this new thing called HEY, HEY.com email service, because we just felt like we had to make more things again. (01:01:04): This idea that I thought, that we could be happy as a company just doing one thing really well, which was a major shift. We had multiple products. We basically wound those down. We didn't ever close them down. People can still use them, who were using them before, we just stopped selling them. We even changed the name of the business from 37signals to Basecamp. We're saying, we're signaling all through. We're doing one thing that's just this thing called Basecamp. It's a huge, massive decision to make, and so we were all in on it. And then, a few years ago, we go, "You know what? We're makers. Let's be honest about ourselves." (01:01:39): I'm talking about me, and I was talking about David. But we were just like, "We want to make more things again. We have some more ideas. Why are we suppressing ourselves? Let's not do that." We made HEY and now we're doing ONCE, and we're going to make more products and more products and more products. We're going to probably do another book, as I mentioned earlier. It was that. I think that's the biggest major fundamental 180 degree change that I've changed my mind on, but I changed my mind all the time. (01:02:08): I disagree with myself constantly on small things. Product design decisions or the naming of something, or how we roll something out, or how I'm going to write something or present something or say something. There's probably an answer, I'm sure there's an answer in this podcast that if I listen back, I'd go, "I would probably answered it differently," or, "I don't even agree with the way I answered that." There's a million things like that happening all the time. But in terms of big things, I think that's the best example I can come up with.
turns.zh: 几年前，准确来说是几年前，我们曾同时开发多个产品，但后来决定专注于Basecamp。我曾以为，在职业生涯的剩余时间里，我会满足于只专注于一件事，并尽可能把它做到极致。这就像雕刻一座雕像，不断雕琢、打磨，让它变得越来越完美。我至今依然非常享受在Basecamp上工作的过程。但几年前，我们推出了名为HEY的邮件服务，因为我们觉得自己又该多做些产品了。（01:01:04）：我当时认为，作为一家公司，只要能把一件事做得非常出色就足够幸福了，这是一个重大的转变。我们曾拥有多个产品，但最终将它们逐渐停用。我们并没有彻底关闭这些产品——之前使用过它们的人仍然可以继续使用，只是我们不再销售这些产品了。我们甚至将公司名称从37signals改为Basecamp。我们想传达一个信息：我们专注于做一件事，叫做Basecamp。这是一个重大而艰难的决定，所以我们全力以赴。几年前，我们突然意识到："我们是创造者，还是诚实面对自己吧。"（01:01:39）：我说的是我自己，也包括大卫。但我们当时想："我们想再多做些产品。我们有更多想法。为什么要压抑自己呢？别这样。"于是我们推出了HEY，现在又在做ONCE，我们还会继续开发更多产品。正如我之前提到的，我们可能还会有新书出版。这就是最大的转变。我认为这是我改变主意最彻底的一次，但我其实一直在改变主意。（01:02:08）：我经常在一些小事情上与自己意见不合。比如产品设计决策、命名方式、推广策略，或者如何写作、展示或表达观点等。回听这期播客时，我肯定会发现有很多地方我本可以换种说法，或者对自己的回答感到不满。类似的情况每天都在发生。但在重大决策上，Basecamp的例子最能说明问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's clear that you've designed your life and designed your business in this very intentional way. And you've done something very different. You've built a company-
turns.zh: 很明显，你以一种非常有意的方式设计了自己的生活和事业。因为默认的路径——我会参考另一期播客——默认的路径是：创立公司、融资、打造大规模业务、创造大量收入、退出、尝试新事物。而你走了一条截然不同的道路。你创立了一家公司——
