turns.en: Is this what that was? Yeah. I'm moderately familiar with that idea. I didn't listen to that podcast, but I saw some clips. I find it interesting because you've designed your life intentionally. It's funny because there are some principles I hold, perhaps, or some direction I'm headed, but I don't think about any of this ahead of time, including the company. We don't have a multi-year plan. I don't even have a one-year plan. I don't even have a six-month plan or a quarter. We think about everything we're going to do every six weeks. Every six weeks, we rethink what we're going to do next. (01:03:33): We're very much an in-the-now company, making it up as we go. And this is true for me, personally, my career, the whole thing. I didn't have any of this planned out. I didn't decide I wanted to be like this or like that. I just figure out what works and keep doing that until it doesn't. And then, maybe we do something else. But it's very much, I'm not on a path. I can't see the path. I'm on a path. We're going somewhere. I don't want to stand still. But I don't know where I'm going, and I'm perfectly comfortable with that. (01:04:05): For me, it is really much about making it up as you go, based on, again, being in touch with how things feel to you, what your intuition is, what your gut tells you, what makes you happy. What do you want to do? What can you do? Sometimes, it's things that make you happy and you can't do, just because life is what it is. So, understanding that and figuring out what the trade-offs are. But really, it's figuring out as we go, and I think, frankly, it's the best way to run a business. I think it's the healthiest, most honest way to run a business, which is, to figure it out as you go. (01:04:37): I think the further out you plan, the less you know about the decisions you're making. And by the time you get there, you're probably going to be wrong, or you're going to want to do something else. And then, if you're like, "Don't do those things," then what's the point of planning? People end up doing things they don't want to do because they said they were going to do them. Obligations in the future, I think, are quite dangerous, and I think they send people down a path of unhappiness, actually. I think just staying closer to now is probably the best way to do that.
turns.zh:
是这样吗？对啊。我对这个理念还算熟悉。我没听过那个播客，但看过一些片段。我觉得很有意思，因为你是有意设计自己生活的。说来有趣，我可能也有一些坚持的原则，或者确定的发展方向，但我从不提前规划任何事——包括公司业务。我们没有多年规划，甚至没有一年规划，更没有六个月或季度规划。我们每六周会重新评估下一步的行动方向。（01:03:33）我们是一家顺势而为的公司，包括我个人职业生涯在内的方方面面都是如此。我从未刻意规划过未来，不曾决心成为某种特定样子。我只是摸索出有效的路径，持续前行直到失效。然后，也许我们会尝试别的方法。我没有既定的人生轨迹，也看不清未来的路径，但我乐在其中。我在前行，而非停滞不前。虽然不知道终点在哪，但这份未知感恰恰让我感到自由。

（01:04:05）对我来说，关键在于顺势而为，时刻倾听内心的声音——感受当下情绪，追随直觉，追寻快乐。想做什么？能做什么？有时，有些美好的愿景因现实阻碍而搁浅，但坦然接受现实，权衡取舍才是明智之举。坦率地说，这是经营企业的最佳方式，也是最健康、最真诚的经营之道。

（01:04:37）我认为越是长远规划，越容易偏离初衷。到头来，你要么错判形势，要么后悔当初的选择。若被固有计划束缚，规划还有什么意义？人们往往因遵守承诺而做着违背本心的事，未来责任感实则暗藏危险，常令人深陷不快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of this trickles down from the biggest decision you made, which is, don't raise money, keep control of this business. You're the boss. There's no boss above you.
turns.zh: 这一切都源于你做过的最重要决定——不融资，牢牢把控公司主权。你才是老大，而上头没有更高权威。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah, the independence. If you go to 37signals.com, there's 37 ideas. And the first one, there's a 00, which is start here, which is like a read me. But 01 is independence. Independence is the root of all the things we're able to do, and we did make that intentional decision. We didn't know all the tentacles that come up from that and what it's going to impact and touch, but we knew principally, we want to be able to do what we want to do. (01:05:40): We want to be entrepreneurs and to me, that means working for yourself. The moment you go out and take money or have these big obligations, you end up working for someone else. I do understand why some companies do it, but I don't understand why a lot of people do it, who probably shouldn't do it. I think staying independent is a wonderfully fulfilling experience, and it's very hard to do when you're beholden to someone else's timeframe and expectations. (01:06:12): Another thing we rarely have here are expectations. This is the point. We launch a new product, I don't know what's going to happen. We launched Basecamp, I didn't know what was going to happen. We launched HEY, I didn't know what was going to happen. We're going to launch some new stuff soon, I don't know what's going to happen. We don't say, "If this gets 20,000 users, then it's a success." I don't know. We don't care. It doesn't even matter. (01:06:33): We're making it anyway, and we're going to see what's going to happen. The market will tell us what happens. I'll just wait to find out. There's no sense in spending the time thinking about what could be.
turns.zh: 是的，独立性。如果你访问37signals.com，会看到37个理念。第一个理念是00，标题是“从这里开始”，类似于“读我文件”。但01是独立。独立是我们能做成一切事情的根基，我们有意做出这样的选择。我们当时并不知道这会带来怎样的连锁反应，影响和触动哪些方面，但我们深知，关键在于我们要能做自己想做的事。（01:05:40）我们想成为创业者，对我来说，这意味着为自己工作。一旦你去融资或背负重大义务，最终就会为别人工作。虽然我理解有些公司这么做，但我不理解很多本不该这样做的人为何要这样。我认为保持独立是一种极其充实的体验，而当你受制于别人的时间表和期望时，做到这一点非常困难。（01:06:12）我们这里很少有期望。这才是关键。我们推出新产品时，我不知道会发生什么。推出Basecamp时，我也不知道会怎样。推出HEY时，我同样毫无头绪。很快我们又要推出新产品了，还是不知道结果如何。我们不会说：“如果能吸引2万用户，那就算成功了。”我不知道，也不在乎。这根本无关紧要。（01:06:33）我们还是会去做，然后看看结果如何。市场会给出答案。我只需静待结果。没必要花时间去预测可能的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to push back, I imagine there are expectations of like, "I hope this works out. I hope people adopt it. I hope it becomes the best email client in town." There's a sense of like, "We want this to succeed"?
turns.zh: 我要反驳一下，我觉得还是有期望的，比如“希望这个能成功，希望人们会采用它，希望它能成为市面上最好的邮件客户端”。总会有种“我们希望这个能成功”的心态吧？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: That's pride, though. That's a matter of like, we want to be proud of the work that we did. We really hope people like it, and we want to keep doing it. To me, that's a sense of caring about the work itself. It's not so much about the outcome, which you don't control as much as you might think. Clearly, we want people to accept the work that we do and we want to find enough people who like it to make it sustainable, but I don't have them in mind. This is going to sound selfish, but I have me in mind first. Because if I'm not for me first, it's hard to be for someone else. (01:07:29): I'm for us. We want to make things that we're proud of, that we think are really good, that are unique, that brings something new to the world that doesn't exist, otherwise there's no point in doing it. That bring a different perspective that only we can provide because everyone has their own. We want to make sure ours is very visible in the products that we make, which is why we approach things very differently than most, and our products are very different than most. That's why they should be there. We should provide alternatives. (01:07:56): As I said earlier, I don't like the word competition, because it almost sounds like you could be making the same thing. I want to provide an alternative, which is a different approach, a different way forward. It could be in pricing. It could be in the way something works. It could be in the flows in the thing. It could be the entire conception of the thing, but it should be an alternative. If it's not an alternative, it doesn't need to exist. Anyway, that's how I think about it. (01:08:24): But yeah, there are expectations. Or I should say, maybe it's more like there are desires and hopes of acceptance to some degree, because it needs to. Otherwise, we can't stay in business. But really, it's like, are we proud of it first? We're wrapping up the HEY calendar right now, which is the calendar we're building for our HEY email service. I'm really proud of it. I have no idea what's going to happen. It's very unusual. But I'm really proud of the work that we did, and that's enough for me. (01:08:47): I think it's going to do well. I don't know, though, and it doesn't really make any sense to wonder if it will or not. It just, it will or it won't. All I can do is, be proud of the work that we're doing and be proud of the people who are doing it, and feel like we're putting something out in the world that we think should be here. Whether or not people agree is up to them.
turns.zh:
然而，这就是自豪感。这关乎我们想为自己所做的工作感到自豪。我们真心希望人们能喜欢我们的作品，并希望能持续做下去。对我而言，这意味着要关注工作本身，而不是其结果——你对结果的掌控力远比你想象的要小。显然，我们希望人们认可我们的工作，也希望能找到足够多喜欢它的人，让它能持续发展，但我首先考虑的是自己。如果我不先为自己着想，就很难为他人着想。  
（01:07:29） 我是为我们自己而做的。我们想创造出令自己自豪、认为真正出色的作品，这些作品要独特，要能为世界带来前所未有的新元素，否则做这些事就没有意义了。我们要提供一种只有我们能提供的不同视角。这在我们制作的产品中必须有所体现，这就是为什么我们的做法与大多数人截然不同，我们的产品也与大多数人不同。这就是它们存在的意义。我们应该提供替代方案。  
（01:07:56） 正如我之前所说，我不喜欢‘竞争’这个词，因为它听起来好像你们在做同样的东西。我想提供的是另一种选择，一种不同的方法，一条不同的前进道路。它可能体现在定价上，可能体现在某个功能的实现方式上，可能体现在产品的流程上，甚至可能是整个产品的理念，但它必须是一种替代方案。如果不是替代方案，那它就没有存在的必要。总之，这就是我的看法。  
（01:08:24） 但确实存在期望。或者说，也许更准确地说，是某种程度上的期望和对被认可的渴望，因为这对我们来说是必要的。否则，我们就无法持续经营。但说真的，我们首先要为自己感到自豪吗？我们现在正在完成HEY日历的制作，这是我们为HEY邮箱服务打造的日历。我对它真的很自豪。我不知道会怎样。它很特别。但我为我们所做的工作感到自豪，这对我来说就足够了。  
（01:08:47） 我觉得它会表现出色。不过我也不确定，纠结它是否会成功也没有意义。它要么成功，要么不成功。我所能做的就是为我们正在做的工作感到自豪，为参与其中的人感到骄傲，并觉得我们正在向世界推出一些我们认为应该存在的东西。至于人们是否认同，那是他们的事。

turns.en: Okay. One of them is, work isn't war. You wrote a book about this roughly, about Work Doesn't Have to Suck, but I guess, can you just talk about why war work feels like war, and then what maybe people could do to make it feel less like war?

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: This is about words in a lot of ways. I'm not looking at the page right now. I could pull it up and read it, but essentially, a lot of work uses war metaphors. You're targeting customers. You are conquering a market. Gosh, now I really want to make sure I get all these right. Hang on, I'm just going to look this up. Because these things are how people talk about work. It says, "They conquer the market. They capture mindshare. They target customers. They employ a sales force. They hire head hunters. They destroy the competition. They pick battles and they make a killing." (01:10:10): That's how people talk about business. I find that to be depressing. It just feels depressing to me. We use words to establish a perspective in a way of thinking about the world. And if those are the words that are in your head, then you feel like it's this war. This is the other thing. People are always like, "What do the Navy SEALs do?" And they're like, "Heck, yeah." That's the Navy SEALs, man. It's not your software business. Why are we always looking to Navy SEALs to tell us how to run our business? "The military, they've got a group of eight and they do these." (01:10:42): It's like, "Yeah, okay, that's that context." Can we not look at that for a second about ... That's amazing. What they do is amazing, obviously, but what you're doing is you're making B2B accounting software. Let's just chill for a second here, okay? I like to think of words that are more additive and alternative. " We can exist. Let's exist. Let's make something great." Not, "Let's beat them, let's conquer them, let's make a killing." Let's just make something great. I think that matters, and it changes the way you think about the work that you do. (01:11:16): It's more about pride and excitement and a spirit of creation than it is destruction. I think if you go into it with destruction in mind, you're going to end up in a pretty dark place. That's our point of view.
turns.zh: 很多方面来说，这都与用词有关。我现在没看那页内容，但我可以把它调出来读一读。总之，很多工作都用了战争的比喻——比如“攻击客户”、“征服市场”。天哪，现在我真想确保把这些都理解透彻。等等，我先去查一下相关术语。因为这些词汇正是人们谈论工作时常用的说法。比如，“征服市场”、“占据市场份额”、“锁定客户”、“组建销售团队”、“聘请猎头”、“击败竞争对手”、“挑选战役并大获全胜”（01:10:10）……这就是人们谈论商业的方式。我觉得这很令人沮丧。这些词汇会让人觉得这是一场战争。这也是另一个问题。人们总是问：“海豹突击队做什么？” 对方就会说：“当然了！”但那毕竟是海豹突击队的事儿，跟你的软件业务毫无关系。为什么我们总想借鉴海豹突击队的经验来经营自己的公司呢？“军队里有八个人就能做到这些。”（01:10:42） 这就像在说：“嗯，好吧，那是他们的背景。”我们能不能暂时先别纠结于这些背景知识？他们确实很了不起，但你做的是B2B会计软件啊。我们能不能稍微冷静一下，好吗？我更倾向于选择更具建设性、更具替代性的词汇。比如，“我们可以存在。让我们存在。让我们创造伟大的事物。” 而不是“让我们击败他们，让我们征服市场，让我们大赚一笔。” 让我们专注于创造伟大的事物。我认为这很重要，它会改变你对工作的看法。（01:11:16） 这更多的是关于自豪感、激情和创造精神，而非毁灭欲。若你一开始就带着毁灭的念头去创业，最终只会陷入黑暗的境地。以上就是我们的观点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, I love that. Coming back to this bootstrap path, there's a lot to love about it. Independence, with that trickles down all these things that you're able to do with your company that other companies aren't able to. (01:11:43): For someone that's thinking about going down this path and wants to bootstrap their company, that doesn't have a lot of money because it takes cash to start a business, do you have any advice for just how to get started down this path?
turns.zh: 太棒了，我很赞同。回到自力更生的道路上来，这个路径有很多值得喜爱的地方。独立自主，这会带来一系列好处，让你能为公司做很多其他公司做不到的事。（01:11:43） 对于那些考虑走这条路并想自力更生创业的人来说，创业需要资金，而他们手头资金不足。你有什么建议能帮助他们开启这条路吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah. First of all, it's hard. This is hard. When you have nothing, especially, it depends where you are in your life, too. You may have a couple of kids and you don't have a lot of time, and you got to pay mortgage. It's tough, so this is hard, but it's the reality for almost every business in the world that starts. The best advice I could give you is, and this sounds so trite, but really it's true, is, stay as small as you can for as long as you can. The only thing you can really control are your costs. You can't control the alternatives in the market. The competition, you can't control them. You can't determine the market itself. You can't control the economy. You can't control how much advertising costs, but you control your own costs. (01:12:39): The other thing I would encourage people to do is, figure out how to do as much as they can on their own before they bring on a second person. Really work and struggle through something on your own. The moment you bring on someone else, you've got another mouth to feed. It becomes expensive. You got another personality to deal with the more you rely on them. And if they turn out to be the wrong person, you have to lose them. You don't have anyone to do the work that now you have them doing, and now you've got to do it. You're not going to be any good at it. You got to start as small as you possibly can and do as much of the work yourself as you possibly can. (01:13:11): Keep your costs in check. Don't spend any money on branding. Don't go get an office. Don't spend anything on anything, basically, except the tool you use. Let's say, it's your laptop or whatever you're going to use. Get a good one. They don't cost much anymore. 1,500 bucks or something like that, you can get a really nice MacBook Air or whatever. You need an internet connection and maybe you need a host somewhere or whatever, but use Squarespace to set up your site for 15 bucks a month or whatever. Don't go hire a web designer. Find all the efficiencies and keep your costs incredibly low, and don't make things hard on yourself. (01:13:47): This is the other thing that all businesses at every stage need to keep in mind. While it's hard, things are relatively simple until you make them complicated. Simple can also be hard, but complicated is a lot harder. I think Brian Chesky had a really good bit on this, I think, on your podcast about how companies get complicated. And I loved that. When I was hearing it, I kept hearing this unfolding, this complex shape that you almost can't fold back. It's so complicated now that you don't even see where it came from. Now, it is what it is and you can't put it back in the bottle. It's just a mess, right? This happens really quickly and it can happen at a small scale, too. These are a bunch of things, and none of this is to say it's going to work. You could follow all those things and it could just completely fall apart. And it probably will. It's just the reality. I think something we use at 37signals, David taught me this, it's really a stoic thing, which is just the idea of negative visualization. What's the worst that can happen? You got to be at peace with the worst that can happen. Just role-play that and go, "What's the worst?" For example, we're doing these new ONCE products. What's the worst that can happen? Well, the ONCE model is totally different. It's not SaaS. It's you pay once, you download the software. You install on your own server. (01:15:09): We're putting a lot of effort into this. This could be the wrong time to do it. It could be a total flop. This could not find any traction on the market. What's the worst that can happen? Well, we spent six months exploring something and having a really good time doing it. Our margins are there, so we can do it. I wouldn't suggest someone does this if they can't afford to do it. But we know this might not work, and we're already at peace with the fact that this might not work. That's, I think, how you ultimately are able to move forward, is to be at peace with knowing what's going to happen if it doesn't work out.
turns.zh:
是啊。这首先很困难。这确实很难。当你一无所有时，尤其要看你处于人生的哪个阶段。比如，你可能有几个孩子，时间有限，还得还房贷。这太艰难了，所以这确实很难，但几乎所有初创企业都面临着这样的现实。我能给你的最好建议是——听起来很老生常谈，但确实是真理——尽可能长时间保持小规模经营。唯一你能真正控制的是成本。你无法控制市场的替代方案，竞争对手的策略，你无法左右市场本身，也无法左右经济环境，更无法控制广告费用，但你能控制自己的成本。（01:12:39）另外，我建议大家在引入第二个人之前，先尽可能自己完成更多工作。当你引入他人时，你就多了一个要养活的嘴巴。这会增加开支。你越依赖他们，就越需要应对他们的个性。万一他们不合适，你还得把他们裁掉。原本由他们完成的工作现在就得你自己做，而且你还未必能胜任。你必须从一开始就尽可能保持小规模，自己完成尽可能多的工作。（01:13:11）控制成本。别在品牌推广上花钱。别租办公室。除了你使用的工具，基本别花钱。就拿笔记本电脑来说，现在价格不算贵。1500美元左右就能买到不错的MacBook Air之类的设备。你需要网络连接，可能还需要托管服务之类的，但用Squarespace搭建网站每月只需15美元左右。别请网页设计师。寻找各种节省成本的方法，把开支压到极低，别给自己找麻烦。（01:13:47）这是所有企业在每个阶段都需要牢记的另一条准则。虽然困难重重，但在你把事情复杂化之前，一切都相对简单。简单有时也很难，但复杂则难上加难。我觉得Brian Chesky在你的播客上对公司复杂化的问题讲得很到位，我很欣赏。听他讲的时候，我总能感受到那种复杂的蔓延——那种几乎无法收拾的复杂局面。现在已经复杂到你都看不清起因了。事已至此，就无法再收回了。简直是一团乱麻，对吧？这种情况发展得很快，甚至在小规模时就可能出现这些问题。这些都是需要考虑的因素，但这并不意味着一定能成功。你可能照做，结果还是一败涂地。现实就是如此。我觉得我们37signals团队用的一个方法，David教给我的，叫做斯多葛主义，就是进行负面想象。最坏的情况会是什么？你必须坦然接受最坏的结果。试着设想一下，“最坏的情况会怎样？”比如，我们正在开发新的ONCE产品。最坏的情况是什么？ONCE模式完全不同，不是SaaS模式。用户一次性付费，下载软件，自己安装在服务器上。（01:15:09）我们在这上面投入了大量精力。现在或许时机不对。这可能会彻底失败。这款产品可能找不到市场。
市场上反响如何？最坏的情况能怎样呢？嗯，我们花了六个月时间探索这个项目，过程还挺愉快的。我们的利润空间足够支持这个尝试，所以我们可以承受这个风险。如果做这个项目负担不起成本，我绝不会建议别人尝试。但我们清楚这项计划可能不会成功，而我们早已坦然接受了这种可能性。我认为，最终能推动事情向前发展的关键，就在于坦然接受事情不顺利时的后果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to touch on Linear. One, it's interesting that you guys have a lot of similar philosophies. What is it about project management, task management software that creates this sort of approach to business? That's maybe one question, if there's something there. (01:15:59): And then, the other is, it feels like they have a lot of similar philosophies. Growth isn't a focus. It's gut and instinct. They have paid work trials. They're profitable. They don't spend a lot of time around VC money. (01:16:11): Do you have a feeling like this approach could work in the venture route? And do you see them as maybe an example of like, "Hey, maybe we could adopt a lot of these things and also raise money?" Maybe there's another direction here?
turns.zh: 我想谈谈 Linear。首先，很有趣的是，你们在项目管理和任务管理软件方面有很多相似的理念。是什么让你们形成这种商业模式呢？这或许是个值得探讨的问题。（01:15:59）另外，他们的理念似乎非常相似。增长并非核心目标，他们更依赖直觉和本能。他们提供付费试用，业务已经盈利，不太依赖风投资金。（01:16:11）你觉得这种模式在风投领域也能奏效吗？你是否认为他们可以成为典范，启发我们借鉴他们的许多做法，同时成功融资？或许这条路值得探索？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah. I can tell you I don't know enough about them to comment on their ... I've heard some about them and it sounds like they have some similar points of view. Where those came from, I don't know. Maybe they materialized out of nowhere. Maybe they picked them up from someone else. Maybe they came up with them themselves. Lots of different ways to work. It's nice to hear that other people are trying some of these things and it's working for them, so that's great. (01:16:45): The thing with the VC route, so the idea of having too much money, it doesn't mean you can't work efficiently and thoughtfully. But it does create a degree of sloppiness, because you don't have to. When you don't have to, and when I'm saying have to, you could say have to what? Have to do a whole bunch of things. When you don't have to, we don't have to make money, when you don't have to be efficient, when you don't have to be profitable, you just get sloppy. (01:17:15): "Let's hire some more people. Whatever, we can afford to. In fact, they need us to spend the money, by the way. They didn't give us the money to save it and earn 6% interest." Which would be great now. Three years ago, 0% interest. "They didn't give us the money to sit in the bank. They gave us the money to spend the money." What are you going to spend it on? Two things, people and marketing. Basically, that's what you spend it on. (01:17:36): We can buy more ads. We can do more of this. We're going to do that. We can hire some more people, build up more teams, do more things simultaneously. There's a certain sloppiness in that. I think it just becomes harder when the environment encourages slop, which is why I think the value in bootstrapping is that it teaches entrepreneurs, it not even teaches, it forces them to have to figure out how to make money. The more time under the curve they have making money and practicing making money, the better at it they're going to get. (01:18:07): I used the guitar metaphor a bit earlier, I'll use it again. If you're playing guitar, if I give you a guitar and ask you to go up on stage and play guitar, you're going to suck. It's going to be horribly embarrassing and you're going to be terrible at it. You might be terrible at it a month later, but you'll be slightly better at it. You do it for six months or a year, you're going to be better and better. And then, five years and you're really getting good. Why do we think that a business that is sloppy, that doesn't have to make their own money, that is just getting pumped full of money by somebody else, can all of a sudden turn on the profit spigot and all of a sudden be profitable? (01:18:36): What you see is that they oftentimes cannot because they're just not set up to be that way. They've never played guitar before, and now they're being asked to play guitar. The reason I think it's great for entrepreneurs to start bootstrapping is because they just have more practice making money. They get better and better and better at the fundamental skill you need to have ultimately to run a successful business, which is to make money. If you don't have to do that from the start, you're just not practicing that. You're practicing spending money. (01:19:02): Getting good at spending money is not a valuable skill as getting good at making money. That's why I think it's just harder. But, of course, it's possible. It's just harder.
turns.zh: 是啊。我可以告诉你，我对他们了解得不够多，不好评判他们的……我听说过一些关于他们的消息，听起来他们有些相似的观点。但这些观点从何而来，我不知道。也许他们是凭空产生的，也许是从别人那里借鉴来的，又或许是自己独立思考出来的。各种不同的工作方式都有。很高兴听到其他人尝试这些方法并且取得了成效，这真是太好了。（01:16:45）：关于风险投资路线的问题，拥有过多资金并不意味着你不能高效、谨慎地工作。但这确实会导致某种程度上的松懈，因为你没必要这样做。当你没必要这样做时——我说的"必须"，指的是必须做什么？必须做一大堆事情。当你没必要这样做时，我们不必赚钱，不必追求高效，不必盈利，就会变得松懈。（01:17:15）："再招些人。管他呢，反正我们负担得起。事实上，他们还要求我们花钱呢。毕竟，他们给我们的钱不是让我们存着、赚6%的利息的。"现在赚6%的利息倒是不错了。三年前可是0%的利息啊。"他们给我们的钱不是让我们存银行的，而是让我们花掉的。"那花在什么地方呢？两个方面，人力和营销。这基本上就是花钱的方向。（01:17:36）：我们可以投放更多广告，开展更多活动。这些我们都会去做。可以多招些人，组建更多团队，同时开展多项工作。这种松懈的作风确实存在。我认为，当环境鼓励松懈时，难度就会增加。这就是为什么自力更生的价值所在——它教会创业者，迫使他们必须想办法赚钱。创业者在赚钱和实践赚钱方面投入的时间越多，他们就会越擅长。（01:18:07）：我之前用过吉他比喻，现在再说一次。如果你弹吉他，我给你把吉他，让你上台表演，你肯定弹得很烂。这会非常尴尬，表现很糟糕。一个月后你可能还是很烂，但会稍微好点。坚持六个月或一年，你就会越来越好。五年后，你就会真正弹得很好了。为什么我们认为一个松懈的企业，不必自己赚钱，只是被别人注入资金，就能突然开启盈利模式，变得盈利呢？（01:18:36）：现实情况是，他们往往做不到，因为他们根本没有这样的准备。他们从未弹过吉他，现在却被要求弹吉他。我认为创业者从自力更生开始很重要，因为他们在赚钱方面有更多的实践。随着实践，他们会越来越擅长经营成功企业所必需的基本技能——赚钱。如果从一开始你就不必这样做，你就不会去练习。你只会练习花钱。（01:19:02）：擅长花钱可不像擅长赚钱那样有价值。这就是为什么我觉得这更难。但当然，也不是不可能。只是更难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing is, essentially, to do this well. You need discipline. Understand, here's the incentives they're driving me to; spend more money, grow faster, and being really good at not ... And then, also, it sounds like you just need investors that are on board with ... "We understand. We're not going to focus on growth obsession. We're not going to focus on getting new teams. We're going to give you space to build it the way you want."
turns.zh: 我的理解是，关键在于要把这件事做好。这需要自律。要明白，现有的激励机制迫使我必须做到以下几点：投入更多资金、加速增长、还要擅长不做某些事…… 听起来你需要的投资者必须认同……“我们理解。我们不会执着于增长狂热。我们不会急于组建新团队。我们会给你足够的空间，让你按照自己的方式来打造业务。”

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: That exists. It's just also an outlier in that industry. I think what you need are constraints, is what I'm actually trying to get at. You need constraints. When you have just loads of money, you basically have very few constraints. That's what tends to lead to slop. Versus like, "Hey, if we don't figure this out, we can't make payroll next week or next month." You just start to figure things out. One of the best stories I heard about this was Peter Rahal, who started RXBAR. Are you familiar with RXBAR?
turns.zh: 这种情况确实存在，但在该行业中实属异类。我认为真正需要的是约束条件，这才是我想传达的核心理念。你需要约束。当资金充裕时，约束条件就变得极少。这往往导致决策草率。而当面临“如果下周或下个月发不出工资，我们就得裁员了”这样的紧急情况时，你才会开始理清头绪。我听过的最佳案例之一，是Peter Rahal创立RXBAR的故事。你熟悉RXBAR吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah, little protein bars or whatever. There's a great article about this years ago, where he was talking to his dad about, I think, raising money or something. His dad's like, "Hey, go sell 1,000 fucking bars and come back and talk to me." He's like, "Just sell some fucking bar. Get out on the street and sell some bars, man. You've got products? Sell products. Go, sell." Versus all the things you could possibly do. "Go sell some bars." It's just such great advice and it just cuts through all the crap. I like that scrappiness, and you don't get scrappiness from having large S. You just don't. It's just too easy not to have to do anything. (01:20:46): Not to say that VC companies aren't doing things. They're doing a lot of things, obviously, but are they honing the scrappy skills? Are they learning how to make money and have margin and be profitable? If they don't have to, they probably are not. I think at some point, and we're starting to see this now, this is not like an I-told-you-so thing, this is just, this is what happens. This is not me. This is just economic cycles. Money's harder to find, it's harder to get. Even companies who've raised money, investors are not necessarily putting in additional rounds. There's deep cuts happening, layoffs, pain and suffering. (01:21:23): It's hard to switch from having a lot to not having enough, and then having to work as if you know what to do. I think there's a lot of confusion in the market now, at companies now, I should say, because they don't know what to do. They haven't had to do it before. I feel for them in a sense because, how could they be expected to know what to do? Just frankly, as I said earlier, if someone dropped 10 million bucks on me and 1,000 people, I would have no idea what to do with that. Truly, I would not. I would waste it is what I would do. If you don't have the experience, how are you going to know?
turns.zh: 对，就是那些小蛋白棒之类的产品。多年前有一篇很棒的文章，讲他和父亲讨论融资之类的事情。父亲说：“去卖1000根该死的蛋白棒，然后再回来找我。”他回应道：“去卖些该死的蛋白棒。出去街头卖吧，你有产品？那就去卖啊。”而不是去想各种复杂的解决方案。“去卖些蛋白棒。”这才是明智之言，直击要害。我欣赏这种拼劲，而大公司往往缺乏这种拼劲，因为他们无需为生存而奋斗。（01:20:46）：这并非说风投公司无所作为。显然他们做了很多事，但他们是否在磨砺这种拼劲？他们是否在学习如何盈利、实现利润率和盈利能力？如果没必要，他们很可能不会这样做。我认为某种程度上——现在我们开始看到这种情况了——这并非故作姿态，而是现实写照。这不是我的观点，而是经济周期使然。资金越来越难筹集，投资者也不再追加投资。裁员、痛苦和煎熬正在上演。（01:21:23）：从资金充裕到资金短缺，再到必须像知道该怎么做一样去行动，这转变太难了。我认为现在市场上有很多困惑，尤其是在企业层面，因为他们不知道该怎么做。他们以前从未经历过这种情况。我对他们深表同情，因为怎么能指望他们知道该怎么做呢？说实话，就像我之前说的，如果有人给我1000万美元和1000名员工，我根本不知道该怎么用。这真的会被我浪费掉。如果你没有经验，又怎么能知道呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm the same way with the newsletter and the podcast. There's no way I can grow this thing with money, really. I've tried a bunch of little experiments and nothing really does anything. It actually comes back to, let me find this quote that you have of just your business strategy in a nutshell. "Just keep making great shit. Keep your cost in check. Charge appropriate prices for your work. Share as much as you can and let the chips fall where they may."
turns.zh: 我在新闻通讯和播客方面也有同样的体会。靠钱是根本无法让这些项目发展壮大的。我尝试过很多小规模的实验，但效果甚微。这最终归结到，我想找出你提到的简明商业策略的引语：“继续做出优质产品。控制成本。为你的工作收取合理费用。尽可能多地分享成果，顺其自然。”

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: That's basically it. One of the things I don't think I said in there was, enjoy it. Have fun. Enjoy the ride. Love who you're working with and create a great environment to do great work, and so other people can do great work and thrive as well. That's all baked into that. It's not like, set targets. It's not, try to be a billion-dollar business. It's not, aim for an exit. It's not, be on the cover of whatever. It's not many of those things. (01:22:52): Maybe it's the Midwesterness in me, growing up in Chicago. I don't know. It's just that. The best business advice I ever got, I got from my dad. It's just a simple line. It's like, "No one ever went broke making a profit." And maybe that's just my guiding light, ultimately. It's like, because you can go broke generating a lot of revenue. A lot of companies do. But you can't go broke generating a profit, and I think it's just really tight.
turns.zh: 基本就是这些。我觉得我之前没提到的一点是，享受这个过程吧。玩得开心。享受这段旅程。热爱与你共事的伙伴，为他们创造一个能出色完成工作的环境，这样其他人也能有所建树。这都是融入其中的理念。不是设定目标，不是试图打造价值数十亿美元的企业，也不是急于退出市场，更不是渴望登上某个封面之类的。（01:22:52）：也许是因为我在芝加哥长大，骨子里有种中西部人的特质。我不知道，就是这样。我得到过的最好的商业建议，来自我的父亲。只是一句简单的话：“没有人会因为盈利而破产。” 这或许就是我最终的指引灯吧。因为即使收入很高，也可能破产，许多公司都如此。但盈利却不会导致破产，我觉得这道理再简单不过了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a great quote. Final question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. Let's talk about ONCE. This is a new product/umbrella of products you're developing. Can you just talk about the thinking here? And then, I think you guys are announcing the actual first product within this umbrella?
turns.zh: 真是个很棒的引语。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后一个问题。来谈谈ONCE吧。这是你们正在开发的新产品/产品系列。能谈谈背后的思路吗？然后，我想你们很快就会宣布这个产品系列的首款产品吧？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah. The idea behind ONCE is, David and I feel like, we're probably a bit early here, but we feel like there's going to be a bit of a turn back towards the way things were. Pendulums always swing. And for the last decade or so, SaaS has been pretty much the only way to run business software. Basically, you rent it. There's really not a lot of alternatives. You rent software. We think that there's subscription fatigue and also some benefits to that, for sure, but there's also a lot of downsides just to ...
turns.zh: 是的。ONCE背后的理念是，大卫和我觉得，虽然现在可能还为时过早，但我们预见到行业会出现回归传统模式的趋势。钟摆总会摆动。在过去十年左右，SaaS几乎成了企业软件的唯一运营模式。基本上就是租用软件，几乎没有其他选择。我们认为用户对订阅模式已经产生了疲倦感，虽然这模式确实有其优势，但也有很多弊端……

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: ... that, for sure, but there's also a lot of downsides to subscription software. You keep paying the same amount every month for the thing that you had last month. It's not like a magazine where every month you get literally a new issue. So that's new. I'm paying for new weekly or monthly, okay, that makes sense. I mean, I know there's new stuff that comes out in software products but let's face it, the core of the thing that you're using, 90% of the time is the thing you've been paying for four years now, every month. It just seems like, nah. So we are going to launch this thing called Once, which is essentially a brand and umbrella, a line, a product line of non-SaaS products, of products, not services, things people will download, software business offer products, people will download, pay for once and then install on their own server or a shared server or in the cloud, their own cloud or whatever. (01:24:53): But they'll run it, they'll manage it, they'll pay for it once and there's no subscription fees, no recurring fees. They get updates, they get support and some of that stuff, but that's it. And so we're going to launch the first one shortly here and then we plan on doing, hopefully, maybe three more next year. And the beauty of these things is that what we're basically doing is we're going out in the market and looking at it, although we already know it because we've been in this world. But we're saying, what are the commodities out there? There are a lot of commodities in business software and there's like 50 alternatives and they're kind of all sort of the same yet they're all still charging luxury prices. In my opinion, if you're paying tens or hundreds of dollars a month or in some cases, thousands of dollars a month, month after month after month after month after month for when there's hundreds of alternatives and there's no price differentiation really between them, that's an opportunity. In every other industry, there's generic peanut butter, there's generic pencils, there's generic everything in a sense. (01:25:50): So we're out there looking for commodities that are still charging luxury prices that we can create really beautifully tight, simple, essential generics of very high quality that don't do everything that the other products do, but get the core of it right, the 80-20, we get that right at a high degree of quality. And we can build these in typically three months each with two people. And the maintenance cost is zero to us, essentially. There's no marginal cost here because we make the software and we sell it and we don't have to maintain it in terms of hosting and the whole thing, which is what the expensive part of SaaS is. So anyway, that's the idea behind Once. And we, again, don't know what the market's going to think. I have no idea but we're really excited about trying this and seeing what happens.
turns.zh:
没错，但订阅软件也有很多弊端。你每个月都要为上个月用过的软件支付相同的费用。这不像杂志，每个月都会有全新的内容。所以这很不一样。我付钱获取新功能，每周或每月更新一次，这还说得过去。但说实话，你使用的核心功能，90%的情况下都是你四年来每月支付费用的产品。似乎没必要继续订阅。所以我们要推出一款名为Once的服务，本质上它是一个品牌和产品线——非SaaS产品线——用户可以下载、安装在自有服务器或共享服务器、云端等环境中，无需订阅费或重复付费。用户能获得更新和支持服务，但仅此而已。（01:24:53）：我们很快就会推出首款产品，明年计划再推出三款。这类产品的妙处在于，我们深入市场调研，虽然身处这个行业已久，但仍能发现商业软件领域存在大量同质化产品。市面上有五十款类似产品，却都标着高价。依我看，当数百款产品毫无价格差异时，每月却要支付数十甚至数百美元、甚至上千美元的订阅费，这就是商机所在。其他行业有普通的花生酱、铅笔等商品，某种意义上都是如此。
（01:25:50）：所以我们寻找那些仍标着高价的同质化产品，打造高质量的精简核心产品。这些产品不追求面面俱到，而是抓住核心功能——80/20法则。我们能以极高质量完成开发，每款产品通常只需两人三个月即可完成。维护成本基本为零，因为我们自产自售，无需承担托管等高昂SaaS成本。总之，这就是Once背后的理念。我们也不确定市场反应如何，但对此充满期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then could you talk about the first thing you're launching or is that not out?
turns.zh: 那能否谈谈你们首款推出的产品？还是说还没上线？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah, sure. The first product we're going to be launching is basically an old product that we made way, way, way back when. So years and years and years ago, 2006, we launched a product called Campfire, which was-
turns.zh: 当然。首款产品是我们很久以前开发的——2006年推出的Campfire，当时是一款——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, of course.
turns.zh: 哦，当然记得。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: ... a group chat tool.
turns.zh: ……一个群聊工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How could you not remember Campfire?
turns.zh: 你怎么会不记得Campfire呢？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Well, some people are-
turns.zh: 嗯，有些人——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are younger.
turns.zh: 年龄更小。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: ... 22 and they don't know, understandably so. But if you've been around, maybe you remember Campfire, which was a group chat tool, which is I think eight years before Slack came out or something like that. So it was really early and it was really hard to get people to even understand what this thing was, and a lot of people didn't get it. And then Slack came out, of course, and steamrolled it and really, really executed beautifully and did a great job. But chat has become a commodity. There are a million ways to chat with people now, and in the business realm, they're all still quite expensive and they're all month to month to month. You got Slack, you got Teams, and you've got a few others and it's like, you know what... And there are some open-source alternatives, by the way, that are free or cheap. But we want to put something back out there. (01:27:41): So we're going to relaunch Campfire under the Once brand. You'll pay for it once, you'll install on your own servers, and you'll run it. And it'll do 90% of the things that you want to do every day and these other chat tools and do them very, very well and very, very simply and very, very easily. And we think it's going to be really interesting. And by the way, the other thing we're thinking about with these Once products, which is interesting, just get to this alternative point of view, is that these don't necessarily need to replace things. They can be in addition to. You might still run Slack at your company but you want to back up for when Slack goes down, or you want a special air-gapped chat for your executive team that cannot be leaked by another company where you're hosting data or having other people involved that might have access to it by accident. (01:28:34): You can run things, you can have different tools doing similar things but for different groups in different contexts. Now, you probably wouldn't want to pay month to month to month to month to month for a backup system when something almost never goes down, but if you only have to pay for it once, it might be really... that's a good thing to have. That's an insurance policy to pay for it once and we just have it in our back pocket. The other thing we're doing with Once product is that you get the code. And so if you're a product team and you're curious to see how this product was built, and we've gone to great lengths to make it exceptionally well-built for this purpose, this is a book, essentially, of how to build this kind of thing really, really, really well on the CSS on the HTML and the Ruby on Rails side, for example. (01:29:18): So you'll get all the code and you can look at it and you can modify it, you can play with it and you can tweak it. You can't resell it. There's a certain licensing but it's yours. And so if you want to change the layout, go ahead. If you want to add some features, go ahead. If you want to mess around, go ahead, it's yours. And that's another thing that's really novel. You don't get that in subscription software. So there's a lot of things going on that we're trying. There's some other really cool stuff. I'll tell you, one more quick thing about it is that we're trying to make this first prompt especially have as few words as possible, maybe 30 words. So we're picking tools that are... or picking categories that people already know how to use, and so we're trying to keep as many words out of this as possible so it's instantly essentially available for the entire world. (01:30:05): It doesn't have to be localized. It's just like, it's universal software. We're trying to think about it this way. And when we do have a word, we're going to have a panel that shows that translation in a bunch of different languages. So it's not like you install this pack or that pack, it's like, you can hit this because different people in the world work in different countries. So we have people in different countries that work for us. I don't want to just have the Indian version because people in India might also have people that work in Brazil and they need the Portuguese version. So you can see all the different languages for certain words when we use them, which is a really novel thing. (01:30:34): We're kind of playing, this is the whole thing like, these tools give us a chance to play and explore new realms and new ideas that we couldn't do with SaaS. This is one of the things I'm getting back to the first question you asked me, I think, or maybe it wasn't the first, but this is why I'm excited again. There's some novelty again, there's some new explorations again. We're able to do things that we couldn't do in other places. So there's an excitement that's building around this creative exploration again, and that's really firing us up.
turns.zh:
……他们22岁，可能还不太明白这是怎么回事。但如果你曾参与过相关领域，或许还记得Campfire这款群聊工具。它比Slack问世早了八年左右，当时真的很难让人们理解这项服务的价值，很多人都无法理解它的意义。随后Slack横空出世，势如破竹般占据了市场，执行得极为出色。但如今群聊已成为商品化服务，市面上有无数聊天工具可供选择，尽管在商业领域它们大多价格不菲且采用按月订阅模式。Slack、Teams等产品层出不穷，但说实话……还有一些开源替代方案，价格低廉或免费。但我们想推出自己的产品。（01:27:41）：所以我们将以Once品牌重新推出Campfire。用户只需一次性付费，将其安装在自有服务器上自主运行。它能满足日常90%的需求，功能强大、简洁易用。我们认为这会很有趣。顺便说一句，关于Once产品，我们还考虑了另一种思路——它们不必取代现有工具，而是作为补充方案。比如，企业可能仍在使用Slack，但需要备份服务以防Slack宕机；又或为高管团队打造专属空降聊天室，避免数据泄露给托管数据的第三方公司。（01:28:34）：不同场景下，不同团队可以使用不同工具。显然，你不会愿意为几乎永不宕机的备份系统支付月费，但一次性付费就很划算了。这就像一份保险单，买一次就够了。Once产品还提供源代码。若你身为产品团队，渴望了解这款产品的构建方式，我们下了很大功夫确保其架构符合开发规范。例如，在CSS、HTML和Ruby on Rails等技术层面，这本质上就是一本关于如何打造优质产品的指南。（01:29:18）：你将获得完整源代码，可自由查看、修改、玩味和优化。但禁止转售。虽有特定授权，但源代码归你所有。想调整布局？请便。想添加功能？随意。想折腾？没问题。源代码属于你。这也是创新之处——订阅软件可没这种自由。还有许多尝试中的新功能，比如首页提示语尽量精简至30个字。我们选择易用工具，避免术语障碍，让产品全球通用。（01:30:05）：无需本地化。这是一款通用软件。
就是这样。当我们有了一个单词时，我们会用一个面板把它翻译成多种不同的语言。不是说你要安装这个或那个翻译包，而是你可以直接点击，因为世界上不同国家的人们有不同的工作环境。我们在不同国家都有员工。我不想只提供印度版本，因为印度人可能也在巴西工作，他们需要葡萄牙语版本。所以当我们使用某些单词时，用户可以看到所有不同语言的翻译结果，这真是件新鲜事儿。（01:30:34）我们正在不断尝试，这些工具给了我们机会去探索新的领域和新的创意，这是SaaS无法做到的。这正是我想回到你最初的问题的原因，或许不是第一个问题，但这就是我再次兴奋的原因。又有了一些新鲜事物，又有了一些新的探索。我们能够做一些在其他地方无法做到的事情。因此，围绕这种创造性探索的热情正在升温，这真的让我们充满激情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's clear how you're excited about this. You're saying how you thought you'd be happy just building Basecamp for the rest of your life, and clearly, there's a pull here, I'm going to try something totally new and different. Also, the domain is awesome, Once.com, right?
turns.zh: 很明显你对此充满热情。你提到原本以为自己会一辈子专注于开发Basecamp，但显然现在有种冲动——想尝试全新的、截然不同的东西。还有那个域名Once.com，真是超棒的！

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah, that was fun. And we're still going to do Basecamp in here. So we're still doing SaaS. I still believe in SaaS. This is not going to replace SaaS but there should be an alternative. People should be able to buy what they need versus rent what they need.
turns.zh: 是啊，那段经历挺有趣的。不过我们仍会继续深耕Basecamp领域，所以我们还是会专注于SaaS模式。我始终坚信SaaS的价值。它不会取代现有SaaS，但应该提供另一种选择。用户应该能按需购买所需服务，而非按月租用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is going to be an interesting experiment because this is how we started with software and then SaaS came and everyone loved this idea of, I don't have to worry about anything. I'm just going to pay you monthly and you take care of maintenance and hosting all that stuff and keep updating me with better features. So I think it'll be interesting to see if we've missed something leaving that world. One clarifying question, for updates, do you buy yearly, like a new Campfire every year, or how does that work if there's updates?
turns.zh: 我觉得这会是一次有趣的尝试，因为我们最初是从软件起步的，后来SaaS模式兴起，人们都青睐"无需操心一切"的理念——每月付费就能享受维护、托管等服务，还能不断更新功能。所以很想看看我们离开SaaS世界后是否遗漏了什么关键点。再问个细节，关于更新，你们是每年购买新版本吗？比如每年更新一次Campfire，还是有其他方式？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: So the plan is, is that let's say you buy Campfire 1.0, this is the way software used to work. It's the same approach, which is like, you'll get all the 1.X updates for free. And you'll be able to decide if you want to update yours or not. So we'll say, hey, 1.1 is out and here are the new things and you get to decide if you want to download that and update yours or not. So you can stick with 1.0 if you want or you can skip a version, whatever you want to do. (01:32:19): If when we get to version 2.0, there'd probably be... you'd probably have to buy it again, but we'd probably have a discounted upgrade rate. But that's like, you also totally optional. I don't know if we'll ever even get there. We might not need to. Have no clue. But we're leaving that door open that if there's a radically new version that we had to sink another six or eight months into or something, it feels right to say you'll need to upgrade. Maybe you get half off because you're a previous customer or something like that. So we don't know but that's the plan.
turns.zh: 计划是这样：假设你购买了Campfire 1.0版（这与传统软件模式类似），用户可以免费获得1.X版本的所有更新，并自主决定是否升级。例如，当1.1版本发布时，我们会告知新功能，让用户自主选择是否下载更新。用户可以继续使用1.0版，或者跳过某个版本，随心所欲。（01:32:19）如果升级到2.0版本，可能需要重新购买，但我们会提供折扣升级价。不过这完全可选，我们甚至可能永远不需要这样做。但我们保留这种可能性，万一某个革命性新版本需要投入六到八个月研发，我们可能会要求用户升级。或许会给老用户半价优惠之类的。目前尚不确定，但这就是我们的计划。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's also important for people to remember your target is not to replace Slack at big tech companies, like your market is the Fortune 5 million as you described.
turns.zh: 我认为用户需要记住，你们目标客户并非大型科技公司的Slack替代品，正如你所说，你们的主要市场是《财富》500强中的中小企业。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: First of all, we don't have a sales team, so it's self-service, it'll always be. If some big huge company says... they look at their bill, their Slack bill and they're going, we're paying 1.2 million a year for this? Wait, wait a second, I can pay less than 1,000 bucks once for this. Maybe that's worth having, or maybe even if we don't use it, it's absolutely worth buying because maybe we will use it, or maybe we can experiment with it in this place. One of the things we're trying to do here is find a price point and it's going to be under 1,000 bucks. I won't tell you exactly where, but we're trying to find a price point where it's kind of becomes a no-brainer, like, you know what? We should buy this, we should have, this should be in our toolkit, and we should use this in certain parts of our business even if we don't replace this other thing, although we still might because we might find that as this group or these two groups or three groups that are using this are making exactly the same progress, why are we spending all this money elsewhere? (01:33:53): So it's a bit of a Trojan horse, potentially. I don't know what's going to happen. No idea, but it's going to be pretty interesting. The other thing that's really cool about it, this is the tiniest market in the world, but because it doesn't go out to the internet, you can run it in truly air-gapped research facilities. There was a time way back in the day where the White House got in touch with us. This is when Obama was running and wanted to use Basecamp. But they're like, we need to install it because we can't obviously host this stuff on your servers. I know, I totally get it. We can't do that, unfortunately. Sorry. But they have security needs that are just far beyond what most things allow, but this is the kind of thing where they can actually be completely detached from the public internet and run this kind of software, which is really interesting. Again, tiny market, not what we're building it for, but it's a cool byproduct or side effect, I should say, of running things this way.
turns.zh: 首先，我们没有销售团队，所以这是一项自助服务，永远都是这样。如果某家大型公司看到他们的Slack账单，然后说……他们看了账单，发现每年要花120万美元？等等，等等，我一次性花不到1000美元就能买到这个产品。也许它值得拥有，或者即便我们不使用它，也绝对值得购买，因为说不定我们会用到它，或者可以在某些场景下进行测试。我们现在正试图找到一个价格点，这个价格点必须低于1000美元。我不会具体透露具体数字，但我们正在努力寻找一个价格点，让它变得无需犹豫——比如，你知道吗？我们应该买这个产品，它应该成为我们的工具包的一部分，我们应该在某些业务领域使用它，即便我们不替换现有产品，但我们还是可能会这么做，因为当使用这个产品的两个或三个团队取得完全相同的进展时，我们为什么还要在其他地方花那么多钱呢？（01:33:53）：所以这可能是一种潜在的诱饵。我不知道会发生什么。完全不知道，但肯定会很有趣。另外，这项技术真的很酷，虽然它是全球最小的市场，但由于它不连接互联网，你可以在真正的空中隔离研究设施中运行它。曾几何时，白宫联系过我们。那是在奥巴马竞选期间，他们想使用Basecamp。但他们说我们需要自己安装，因为显然不能在你们的服务器上托管这些数据。我懂，我完全理解。不幸的是，我们无法做到这一点，很抱歉。但他们的安全需求远远超出了大多数产品的承受范围，但通过这种方式运行，他们可以完全与公共互联网隔离开来，运行这种软件，这真的很酷。虽然这不是我们开发它的初衷，但却是以这种方式运行的一个很酷的副产品或附带效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then did you share when this might come out? I know you don't promise dates but is there something you want to share there or is it-
turns.zh: 那么你有没有分享过这个产品可能何时发布？我知道你不承诺具体日期，但你有没有想分享的信息，或者——

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Well, unfortunately, we promised. We said by the end of this year, that's why I was getting to that. But we said by the end of 2023, and we're almost there, here we are in December, so mid-December, we're going to start to roll this out to the first batch of customers. It's probably not going to be available publicly to everyone in the world yet, but that'll come soon after. But the first batch of customers are going to get it and we'll slow-roll it out, figure out what we missed, what we need to tighten up and tweak. It's not really a beta as much as it's just a limited release, which is the smart way to do this, and then we'll open the doors very, very soon after that.
turns.zh: 嗯，不幸的是，我们承诺过了。我们说过年底前发布，这就是我要说的。但我们说的是2023年底，现在已经快到12月中旬了，所以我们将开始向首批客户推出。这项产品可能还不会向全球所有人公开，但不久之后就会开放。不过首批客户会先用上，然后我们会逐步推广，找出遗漏的地方，进行优化和调整。这其实不算测试版，更像是限量发布，这是明智的做法，之后我们会很快向所有人开放。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jason, you're breaking your own rule of not saying by end of the year. Apparently, I learned earlier that that's never works.
turns.zh: 杰森，你违反了自己不承诺年底发布的规则。显然，我之前了解到这从来没成功过。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yeah, it's funny, we definitely said that and we said that six months ago and here we are, end of the year.
turns.zh: 是啊，很有趣，我们确实说过这话，而且六个月前就说过，现在年底了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's happening. So maybe sometimes it works out.
turns.zh: 它要来了。所以也许有时候还是能实现的。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we get to our very exciting lighting round, is there anything else that you wanted to share, touch on, or leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 在我们进入令人兴奋的提问环节之前，你是否还有什么想分享、探讨或留给听众的信息？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I think one of the most important things though to remember, and I got to it in another answer, is just like, humans tend to complicate things, and a lot of things are hard but they're still simple until you make them complicated. And just keep that in mind that you can make a lot of progress with two people, and you can do a lot of great work four weeks at a time max, and you can figure things out as you go, and you don't need to know exactly where you're going, and you can be profitable business, and you can find customers who are willing to pay for things. These are all possible things to do. And you don't need to be a big huge company to be successful. And you don't need to be a big huge company to make significant amounts of money. You don't need to do that. (01:36:42): You don't need to raise money. So it's like, all those things make things more complicated, actually. Some people think they might make them simpler, if I have a bunch of money, it's simpler. It's actually not simpler, it's harder. In a sense, the more... because those things come with expectations and again, they erase your scrappiness, and there are side effects here. Those things come with very, very thick and strong strings attached. And you got to think about what are those strings attach to and what do they prevent you from doing? You don't have a full range of motion anymore. So I'll leave people with that, even if I touched on some of those ideas earlier on.
turns.zh: 我认为最重要的一点——我之前在另一个回答中也提到过——就是人类往往会把事情复杂化。很多事情本质上很简单，但只要你自己把它们搞得复杂起来，就会变得困难重重。要记住这一点：两人合作就能取得很大进展，每次最多四周就能完成大量出色的工作，边做边摸索，不必预知未来方向，也能成功盈利，找到愿意为产品买单的客户。这些都是可行的做法。成功不必依赖大公司，赚大钱也不必非得是大公司。没必要为此筹集资金。（01:36:42）：事实上，这些做法往往让事情更复杂。有些人以为只要有足够资金，一切就会简单化。但实际上并非如此，反而更难了。从某种意义上说，越是依赖外部资源，越会滋生期望，磨灭你的拼劲，还会带来副作用。这些资源附带的条件往往很苛刻。你得审视这些条件的实质，思考它们会束缚你怎样的行动空间。比如，你的行动自由度会被大幅限制。所以最后我想留给大家的思考是：即便我之前提过类似观点，但这些观点依然值得深思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's a really great way to summarize it. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 总结得太到位了。现在我们要进入激动人心的提问环节了。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: The first one is this book here, so Several Short Sentences About Writing. Do you know this book?
turns.zh: 第一本就是这本《写作的几个短句》。你知道这本书吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that book. I have it on my coffee table.
turns.zh: 我超爱这本书。它就放在我的咖啡桌上。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: When anyone ever asks me, what book do you recommend on writing? It's this one, Several Short Sentences About Writing. I can never pronounce his last name, but Verlyn Klinkenborg, I believe is his name, although I might be bastardizing that. But it's an extraordinarily good book about writing and it's all about the sentence, beautifully written, fun to read, really great. The other one is pretty much anything by Derek Sivers, but specifically, Hell Yeah Or No. I recommend this book to everybody. It's really had a big effect on me and David, specifically. We use this term, hell or no, all the time internally. Is this a hell yeah or no? It really clarifies a lot of things. And the last one is this design book, which is interesting. There's a few different versions of it. The one I have handy, it's called Home-made: Contemporary RussianFolk Artifacts. (01:38:35): And what this book is, it's a collection of... it's a beautiful book. It's very simple. Basically, every spread is a person, a story, and a thing that they had to make because they didn't have anything. They couldn't buy what they needed. They didn't have what they needed. So this example here is a guy put a hole in a spoon to make bubbles for his kid, to blow bubbles, large bubbles. This is a TV antenna made out of forks, and it's just like, getting back to the scrappiness, I admire this kind of ingenuity among or over pretty much anything. And I think that this book is full. There's a couple hundred pages. They have a couple different editions of this, but I love this one a lot. Look at this one. This guy had to make a door handle. I mean, in America, we're like, go get a door handle at Home Depot. (01:39:28): This guy didn't have a door handle, so he made it out of a plastic, looks like a gallon oil can or some water thing, and nailed it to a book, which nailed it to a door. Amazing. And this is also why I've always loved... I know this isn't very lightning, sorry but I've always loved looking at jailhouse creations and tools and how people make weapons out of combs and pens. It's just, I find this like, I have nothing, I need something, I can use my human brain to figure out how to make it. I think that scrappiness is beautiful.
turns.zh: 每当有人问我：“你推荐哪本关于写作的书？”我都会回答：“这本《关于写作的几句话》。”我总是记不住他的姓氏，但我觉得他叫维尔林·克林肯伯格，不过可能我把名字记错了。但这本书确实是关于写作的绝佳之作，全书以句子为核心，文笔优美，读来趣味十足，堪称佳作。另外，我还推荐德里克·西弗斯的任何作品，尤其是《太棒了！还是不行？》。我把这本书推荐给所有人。它对我和大卫的影响尤其深。我们现在内部经常用“太棒了！还是不行？”这个短语来做决策。这本书真的让我受益匪浅。还有一本设计书籍也很有趣，有好几个版本。我手边这本叫《自制：当代俄罗斯民间艺术品》（01:38:35）。这本书汇集了大量作品，每页都是一个故事，每个人因为缺乏材料而不得不自己动手制作物品。比如，有个人在勺子上钻孔给孩子吹泡泡，还有用叉子做的电视天线。这让我想起那种在困境中创造的精神，无论面对什么挑战，都能发挥智慧去克服困难。我觉得这本书太棒了，有几百页，不同版本我都爱不释手。看看这页，有个人需要制作门把手。在美国，我们可能会去家得宝买现成的，但这个人没有门把手，就用看起来像一加仑油桶的塑料桶做了一个，还用钉子固定在书上，再固定在门上。太神奇了。这也是我一直喜欢……我知道这有点跑题，但我特别喜欢看监狱里的手工艺品、制作工具，还有人们用梳子和钢笔制造武器的过程。就是那种——我一无所有，需要某样东西，就能动用人类的智慧去创造出来的感觉。我觉得这种创造力真是美妙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was just going to say it speaks clearly to your scrappy mentality. And what is that book called again?
turns.zh: 是啊，这本书显然能体现你的那种不屈不挠的精神。书名叫什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: This one's called Home-made: Contemporary RussianFolk Artifacts. And there's also an Eastern European one and there's another one too, but Home-made.
turns.zh: 这本叫《自制：当代俄罗斯民间艺术品》。还有一本东欧主题的，另外还有一本，但《自制》这本最棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an awesome, unusual selection. Okay, next question. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 真是个独特又令人惊叹的选择。好吧，下一个问题。最近有没有喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I don't watch TV. I rarely get a chance to see movies these days. I really thoroughly enjoyed Oppenheimer though. I mean, I went to the theater to see it, and seeing that in the theater was really special, but I just love the movie, is fantastic.
turns.zh: 我不怎么看电视，现在也很少有机会看电影。不过《奥本海默》我真的很喜欢。我是去电影院看的，在影院看的感觉特别棒，但这部电影本身就很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates that you are interviewing to hire?
turns.zh: 你有没有最喜欢的面试问题，喜欢问被面试者？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: I think we actually went over this one a little bit, which was, I'm always curious about what else... if you had more time, what would you do with this idea? Another one is, whose work do you admire? So it's not so much about what you can do, but what are other people doing that you think is great? I find that, that really illuminates what kind of pulse they have on the world and what they're looking at and what inspires them and what they think is good. So I like that question.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们之前其实已经稍微讨论过这个问题了，那就是，我总是好奇如果你们有更多时间的话，还能对这个想法做些什么？另一个问题是，你欣赏谁的作品？这其实不是在问你能做什么，而是问别人在做什么，你觉得很棒的东西是什么？我发现，这真的能揭示他们对世界的洞察力，他们关注的方向，他们的灵感来源，以及他们眼中优秀的标准。所以我很喜欢这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In that second question, what do you look for? Is it someone that you also admire?
turns.zh: 在第二个问题中，你寻找的是什么？是那些你也钦佩的人吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Ultimately, in the moment, I don't care who it is. It's more about, tell me why. So someone will say, I like so-and-so, I'm like, why do you like them? What are they doing that you think is interesting? This is kind of the thing I tend to always ask, which is, why do you think that that's interesting? I'm always trying to get behind the words and understand where this is coming from because people can prepare answers and they can sound great. But it's like, well, what's behind that? Where are you going with that? Why? What's the genesis of this? That's what I'm always after. And so whether or not I agree with the work or whatever, in the end, it plays a part to some degree but I'm more interested in, how did you get there?
turns.zh: 说到底，当下我并不在意是谁。更重要的是，请告诉我原因。所以有人会说，我喜欢某某人，我会问，你为什么喜欢他们？他们做了什么让你觉得有趣？这正是我常问的问题——为什么你觉得这很有趣？我总想探究背后的逻辑，理解其根源，因为人们可能会准备好答案，听起来很不错。但我想知道，背后的逻辑是什么？你想通向哪里？为什么？灵感从何而来？这才是我一直追寻的。所以无论我是否认同他们的作品，在某种程度上这都无关紧要，但我更感兴趣的是，你是如何得出这个结论的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite product that you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 最近有没有发现的你特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Yes, although it's more of a category. I bought an old car, and I've fallen back in love with stick shifts. I learned how to stick, and then I basically have had automatic cars for many years and I got back into sticks. And now it's even deeper than that. I got back into the old analog driving experience and how wonderful it is to feel attached to the machine that you're using, that you turn the wheel and it turns it rod and it turns the wheels, and that your leg muscle actually is what's breaking the car, to some degree. There's something about that direct feel that really surprised me. It surprised me how much is missing in modern cars and it actually... I like to draw these parallels because this is how I see the world. It reminded me of our business, actually. I think we have a very stick shift business. (01:43:06): We have a very direct business. Everything's very, very tight, very straightforward. There are not a lot of layers of abstractions. There are not a lot of things in the middle between the work we do and the way it feels, and I think of large businesses as automatic transmissions and modern cars where you just... everything's simulated. You don't really know what the road feels like. You can't really feel it in the steering wheel, or maybe there's some fake feel in there now. The brakes are just sending a command to a computer to squeeze the pads. The transmission is like, you don't control it, it just does its own thing. And there's a beauty in that too, but there's also a disconnect that I forgot about until I got back into driving the old car, which is harder to drive and noisier and bumpier and creakier, but there's a real directness to it that's really special, and I think it's actually a good way to look at business and to remind yourself that staying as connected to the thing that you're doing as possible has a lot of value.
turns.zh: 有，虽然更像是一个品类。我买了一辆旧车，又重新爱上了手动挡。我学会了如何换挡，然后多年来一直开自动挡，现在又回到了手动挡。现在这种体验甚至更深层了。我重新体验了那种老式模拟驾驶的乐趣，感觉与正在使用的机器紧密相连——你转动方向盘，带动转杆，转动车轮，腿部肌肉在一定程度上控制着汽车——那种直接的反馈感真的让我惊讶。它让我意识到现代汽车缺失了多少东西，实际上……我喜欢做这种类比，因为这就是我看待世界的方式。这让我想起了我们的业务。（01:43:06）：我们有一种非常手动挡式的业务。一切都非常紧凑、直接。没有太多的抽象层级。在我们所做的工作和实际感受之间没有太多中间环节。我认为大公司就像自动挡的汽车，所有东西都是模拟的。你不知道路面是什么感觉。方向盘上可能也有虚拟的反馈感。刹车只是向电脑发送命令来挤压刹车片。变速箱也是自动控制的，你无法控制它。这也有其美妙之处，但也存在一种脱节感——直到我重新开起那辆旧车，我才意识到这一点。那辆车开起来更困难、更吵、更颠簸、更有噪音，但那种直接的反馈感真的很特别，我认为这也是审视商业、提醒自己尽可能与正在做的事情保持紧密联系的一种好方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome metaphor. Next question, do you have a favorite life motto that you often repeat yourself, share with folks, find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 这真是个绝妙的比喻。下一个问题，你有没有一句最喜欢的的人生格言，经常自我重复、与人分享、在工作或生活中觉得很有用的？

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: And I don't always live up to it, but basically, it's worry less. There's a great Tom Petty lyric. I can't remember which song it's in, but I think it's on Wildflowers on the album. Most of the things you worry about never happened anyway. And it's just so true. I find myself worrying about all sorts of things that don't matter and never happen, and then you're like, God, I spent three days worrying about that, or I went to this appointment and it was fine. The amount of worry, and it's just all in your head, and it's all about anticipating the future that hasn't happened yet, and I try to tell myself that, and I try to tell others that in business. I try to tell myself that in life and in business, but also, I tell others that in business, what if people don't like... I don't know. You'll find out. Worry less about it. It probably isn't going to be a big deal anyway. So that's what I would say.
turns.zh: 我并非总能做到，但基本上，就是少些担忧。汤姆·佩蒂（Tom Petty）有一句歌词，很棒。我不记得是哪首歌了，但我想应该在《野花》（Wildflowers）专辑里提到过。大多数你担心的事情最终都不会发生。这太对了。我发现自己会为各种无关紧要、永远不会发生的事情担忧，然后你就会想，天哪，我为这事担心了三天，或者我去参加了那个会议，结果一切顺利。担忧太多，全是自己想出来的东西，都是在预测尚未发生的未来，所以我试着告诉自己，也试着告诉商界的人：万一人们不喜欢……我不知道。到时候再看吧。少些担忧。反正可能也没什么大不了的。这就是我想说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Worry less.
turns.zh: 少些担忧。

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: Worry less.
turns.zh: 少些担忧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, I was going to ask you this before you mentioned this, but you said you're writing a new book, potentially, are you able to share what this new book might be about?

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: We haven't started writing it. I can tell you, or I'm thinking about it, and it's going to revolve around the idea of gut and intuition in business and decision-making. They're about the opposite in many ways. Whatever, you can't improve what you can't measure, or whatever these things are. And I think that's true in a lot of realms, like medicine, you can look at your biomarkers and you can do things. (01:45:59): I don't think things are quite as direct in business, and I think that intuition and gut is something to be celebrated. So I think what we're probably going to end up doing is looking at all the ways we use intuition and gut to make decisions at work, whether it's hiring or product decisions or policy decisions or whatever it is. Maybe break down some of those decisions in the past, perhaps, or talk about things on a day-to-day basis about how we employ those tools to move forward. So that's roughly the idea. It's very loose right now but hopefully, we can tighten it up and that's what I'd love to focus on that next.
turns.zh: 我们还没开始写。我可以告诉你，或者说我在考虑，书的内容会围绕商业和决策中的直觉与直觉展开。我还不确定这些概念在书中如何呈现，但我认为我们需要更多地赞美商业中的直觉和直觉。大多数商业书籍并非如此。他们在很多方面与之相反。比如“你无法改进无法衡量的东西”之类的。我认为这在很多领域都适用，比如医学，你可以查看生物标志物并采取行动。（01:45:59）但我觉得商业中的情况没那么直接。我认为直觉和直觉是值得赞美的。所以我们可能会探讨在工作中如何运用直觉和直觉来做决策，无论是招聘、产品决策、政策决策还是其他方面。或许回顾过去的一些决策，或许日常谈论如何利用这些工具向前发展。这就是大致的思路。现在还很松散，但希望我们能把它完善起来，这就是我接下来想专注的。

turns.en: Yeah, that would be.

turns.en: Oh, beautiful.

turns.en: Oh, wow.

turns.speaker: Jason Fried
turns.en: This was a few years ago. And I only asked him one question. I was mostly just a student listening to other people's questions. I said, what's your take on doing something well that you know nothing about? Essentially, is there power in being completely ignorant about something? I didn't add this but I've often found myself more creative when I don't know how to do something versus like, well, this is how you're supposed to do it, so you fall into this pattern. And I really loved his answer, which was, "I would just... trust your instinct on that," which is like, a lot of great things happen because you don't know how to do them. (01:47:47): In fact, a lot of innovations happen because you don't know how other people do them, and all you have is your gut. All you have is your intuition. All you have is how you feel about the thing. You don't have evidence, you don't have other examples to follow. You don't have a list of what to do. You just do. And I'm paraphrasing here. But it gave me a lot of confidence and hope to continue to follow our gut. And maybe this is, ultimately, in a way, what was the seed for this book perhaps, although I hadn't really thought about that until now. But it's a beautiful thing to read and to listen to him speak. I love it.
turns.zh: 那是几年前的事了。我当时只问了他一个问题。我基本上就是个学生，听别人提问。我说：“对于你一无所知的事情，你怎么能做好呢？” 本质上，对某件事一无所知反而有力量。（01:47:47）：事实上，很多创新之所以发生，正是因为你不知道别人是怎么做的，你只有直觉。你只能凭感觉行事。你没有证据，没有可效仿的范例，没有操作清单。你就直接行动。我这里是意译的。但这让我更有信心和希望继续遵循自己的直觉。也许这最终就是这本书的种子吧，尽管直到现在我才真正意识到这一点。但读他的文字，听他讲话，是件美好的事。我喜欢。
